s01.slug: MONDAY · 11:40 AM · N. DUPRE STREET, THE ATTIC
body: The light gets to the attic late, and low, and comes in sideways through the gable window past the box fan. Somebody switched it off at dawn; the blades stand still in the frame, and the sun comes through them in one piece for a change and falls the length of the mattresses with the dust hanging in it, going nowhere. Over Jack’s face the nails come down through the roof deck in their rows. This morning the points are dry. It is a Monday, and the house under him is as quiet as a house gets when nobody in it has gone to work.

They got in at ten to six, before the sun. His body has been reporting on Sunday ever since, one item at a time: both knees, from the curb on Esplanade; his voice, gone to gravel somewhere in the fourth quarter and not back up yet; and gold paint in the creases of his left hand that he doesn’t remember getting and that won’t come off on the sheet.

Kevin is awake. He sits on his sleeping bag by the hatch with his back to a rafter, dressed down to the shoes, a paperback of *The Hot Zone* open on one knee and his rosary in the other hand, the crucifix swinging under his knuckles. At seven, while the rest of them slept, he walked to two churches looking for a Monday Mass.
“Two churches,” Kevin says. “Both locked. A *Monday*.”
“City’s sleeping it off,” Jack says, in what’s left of his voice.

“I left a note on the second one.” Kevin finds his page in the Ebola again, and then, without lifting his eyes off it: “That’s acute laryngitis, by the way. Textbook. Rest the voice, push fluids, and no yelling at professional football for six to eight weeks.”
“It’s over. There’s no more football.”
“Then you’re in luck.” He turns a page. “There’s a parade.”

Under the boards the house is going about its Monday at half speed. A pot lid, somewhere. Mémère saying something short in French and the screen door answering on its spring. Out on Dupre Street a car goes by with its horn doing the chant, one tired time, and gives up halfway.

On the middle mattress Theo lies face-down in last night’s good coat with one shoe on. The other shoe isn’t anywhere. His face is pushed so far into the pillow that it looks like a position he has taken and means to defend.

Jack says the penance on his back under Remy’s Tiger, lips going, with no sound to speak of, all the voice he has anyway. *Two by two.* The walking stick. *No food, no sack, no money in their belts.* Sandals, and not a second tunic. *Wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave from there.*
*Whatever place does not welcome you or listen to you, leave there and shake the dust off your feet in testimony against them.*

He says that one again. *Shake the dust off your feet.* And goes on to the end of it, the demons driven out, *and they anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them*, and lies there under the dry nails for a while with his hands on his chest.
The RAZR is on the boards by his ear, where he put it down at six. The little outside screen says he has two.

s02.slug: MONDAY · 12:15 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — AMEN
body: WWL is on the porch rail with the volume up, and it reaches the kitchen through two doors, the front and the screen: a caller from Chalmette who hasn’t slept, telling the host he hasn’t slept, and the host telling him to go to bed and then asking him one more question.

Tony is home. It’s a Monday, a quarter past twelve, and Tony Broussard is in his own kitchen in a Saints T-shirt and house shoes on a weekday, a thing Celeste says hasn’t happened since the market opened back up in ’06. He keeps opening the refrigerator and looking into it, and shutting it, and standing there.
Broussard’s Seafood is shut. Remy drove past it at ten, on his way out for beignets, and reports on the sign taped inside the door in his father’s marker:

body.title: Taped inside the door of Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street (as Remy reports it)
body.text:
CLOSED
WHO DAT
BACK WEDNESDAY
GOD WILLING

body: “The *God willing*’s new,” Remy says. He has powdered sugar down the front of his shirt and the beignet bag in his lap, and he has not offered it around.
“It’s always been there,” Tony says, from behind the refrigerator door. “I just never wrote it down.”
Celeste has taken a personal day from Touro, her first since 2006. She is at the counter in an old Holy Rosary fun-run sweatshirt, writing a list on the back of the light bill.
“The ICU can have me Wednesday,” she says. “God can have me Sunday. Today I’m making groceries.”

The twins went off to school at seven-thirty for a full day, under protest. “Josie told the bus driver school today was against her religion,” Celeste says, still writing, “and he said his too, and took her anyway.”

Down both sides of the table, on the oilcloth, lie eight copies of the *Times-Picayune*. Tony stood in a line of hundreds at a gas station on Carrollton before it was light and came home with them under his arm, and he has laid them out like place cards: one for each of his six children, wherever they are this morning, one for his mother, and one for the girl in the Saints bib at church, and he doesn’t explain the last one. The headline is AMEN, in black letters you could read from the porch.
“Man in front of me bought forty,” Tony says, with his head in the refrigerator. “I said, what for. He said, I’m starting a route.” He shuts the door. “I respect that.”
“Tony,” Celeste whispers, without stopping the pen. “The cold’s for the shrimp.”

In the front room Mémère has hers spread across the arms of her chair and goes over it with a magnifying glass the size of a saucer, from the top of the page to the fold and from the fold to the bottom. When she gets there she lowers the glass and says, “*Bon*.”

It’s Monday, so it’s red beans. The Camellias have been soaking since last night in Mémère’s big pot, and the pickled pork is out on the board in its pink brine, and next to it the onions and the bell pepper and the celery sit in a heap, waiting for somebody.

body.text: Mémère comes in from the front room with her paper under her arm, takes the knife off the board, points it at the onions, and hands it to Jack handle first, without a word, and goes back to her chair. He carries the board to his end of the table and starts.
body.else: Celeste puts the knife in his hand on her way past. “Small, baby.” He carries the board to his end of the table and starts.

body: On the parish calendar by the phone St. Jude is still holding up January.
His coffee is at his elbow, and his toast. Across from him Remy has his AMEN folded back to the sports and is not reading it.

Lena is last. She comes in from the hall in Remy’s purple LSU sweatshirt with the sleeves down over her hands and her hair up in a knot with a pencil through it, takes the corner chair beside his, takes the triangle of toast off his plate without asking, and leans over his shoulder to read the box score with her chin very nearly on it. He moves his coffee so she can get her elbow down. She gets her elbow down. Her sleeve lies along his forearm while she reads, the purple gone soft with a hundred washings, and it stays there while his knife goes.
“Brees,” Jack says, with the knife going. “Thirty-two of forty.”

“Thirty-nine.” She reaches across his onions for the butter. “Thirty-two of thirty-nine. You don’t round a man down in this house, not this week. Hartley, three for three, every one of them from past forty, and Joseph of Cupertino couldn’t get one up from there in a stiff wind. Porter. And the onside kick.” She points his toast at the page. “Payton called it at halftime.”
“You read a box score like it’s the Gospel,” Jack says.
“It’s the day after. It *is* the Gospel.” She takes a bite of his toast and talks around it. “Tomorrow’s the Acts of the Apostles. Wednesday’s the epistles. Everybody gets a letter.”
“*I* called it,” Tony says, from the refrigerator.
“You called it from the porch with your eyes shut,” Celeste says, and underlines something.
Across the table, Remy has been waiting with his mouth full.

body.text: “How’s your Colts fan, brother-in-law?”
body.else: “How’s your girl in Canada, brother-in-law?”

body: Jack shrugs at him over a mouthful of the toast he has left. Beside him Lena’s knife goes on buttering the triangle that used to be his, out to the corners, and she turns the page of his paper with her other hand.
Remy looks round the kitchen for a witness and gets his father. “Leave the man alone,” Tony says. “He’s chopping.”

Laney sweeps in from the hall in a Saints sweatshirt of Tony’s that comes down to her knees, with her hair already done at a quarter past noon in case of cameras. She gets three steps into the kitchen. She looks down the table at the two of them at the end of it, the onions, Lena’s chin, the one paper between his elbow and hers; and she turns round on the linoleum and walks straight back out the way she came. From the hall, low, to Theo, a piece of it comes back through the door:
“— *nobody* move. Not a muscle.”
Theo’s answer, if there is one, doesn’t carry.
At the drainboard Kevin is drying the cup from the bank in Baton Rouge. “Respectfully, the game is over.”
“It is *not* over, Kevin,” Laney says, from the hall.
Margot, at the far end of the table with her notebook open beside her coffee, writes something down and reads it out as she writes it. “Field note. The superstition has outlived its object.”
“*Margot.*”
From the front room, Mémère: “*Qu’est-ce qu’elle a dit?*”
“She said we’re superstitious, Mémère,” Lena calls back, with her mouth full.
A pause in the front room, and the magnifying glass going down on the paper. “She’s learning.”

Remy gets up at last with the beignet bag and goes to the screen door with his keys, and stops there with it open and the radio coming in louder around him. “The team’s landing this afternoon, y’all. Kenner. They’re late, and the whole parish is going.” Behind him on the rail, WWL is still on the man from Chalmette.
Celeste caps her pen. “Making groceries,” she says. “One o’clock. I need a man for the heavy things.”
She is looking at Jack.

journal.title: Remy Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s brother, twenty, LSU. Calls me brother-in-law, and he’s not the one who’s joking. Drives a Suburban like it owes him money. Knew the team was landing before the radio did.

choices.text: *Ask Tony to sign one for your father.*
response: “Mr. Broussard,” Jack says. “Would you sign one for my father?”

Tony lets the refrigerator door swing shut. He looks at Jack, and down the table at his eight papers, and picks one up off the end. “The baby can get her own,” he says. He finds a black marker in the drawer by the phone, takes the cap off with his teeth, and writes across the front under AMEN in big letters that run uphill: *To Frank Costigan, father of the Ohio boy — WHO DAT — A. Broussard.* He blows on it anyway, and reads it over, and nods at it.
“Celeste. Find me a mailing tube.”
She has one, because she has everything. She stands it on the table by Jack’s elbow, and takes the other seven papers up off the oilcloth in a stack against her hip, to set the table for lunch.
“That’s a relic now, Mr. Broussard,” Jack says.
“Second-class,” Tony says, from the refrigerator. “It touched me.”
“You have to be a *saint* for that, Daddy,” Lena says, turning a page. “And dead.”
“Give it time,” says Tony, and shuts the refrigerator on it.
Celeste comes down the table and lifts the papers off it one by one to set it for lunch, every one but the one under Lena’s elbow, which she goes around.

choices.text: *Let her read you the rest of it.*
response: He puts the knife down and lets her have it. She turns his paper back to the front of the sports, settles her chin on his shoulder, and reads it to him, every column, in her debate voice: the drives, the kick, the interception, the box score again for the hard of hearing, at speed and with feeling and with remarks of her own in the margins.
From the front room, through the door: “*Garçon*.”
“That’s what I said, Mémère.”
“You said it like the television. The television is not French.”

Lena says it again, properly, into his collar, and reads on. Celeste waits for the end of a paragraph and slides the paper out from under the two of them to set the table for lunch, and Lena finishes the column from memory.

s03.slug: MONDAY · 1:05 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH
body: Remy’s Suburban is at the curb behind the Odyssey with every window down and WWL on and the engine running, and the sun is out over Dupre Street, bright and not warm, on a man two doors down sweeping gold confetti off his steps into the gutter.
Theo, Laney, Margot and Kevin are already in it. Remy stands at the open back door and counts them with his keys.
“Seven seats,” he says.
“We’re seven,” Margot says, from the way back.
“Kevin can ride on the roof,” Theo says.
“Respectfully —” Kevin says, and Remy shuts the door on it.

Lena is on the top step of the porch with her house keys in her teeth, pulling on her boots. One is on. She works her heel down into the other with both hands on the shaft, frowning at the street and the Suburban and the sky over the roofs out toward the airport, and gets it, and stands, and takes the keys out of her mouth.
“They’re coming *home*,” she says, and takes the steps at a run.
Laney leans out of the middle window with her sunglasses on. “Lena Thérèse Broussard, if you make me miss Drew Brees I will tell your mother about the ninth grade.”
“She knows about the ninth grade,” Lena says from the walk.
“Not *all* of it, she doesn’t.”
Behind Jack, Celeste stands in the front door with her purse on her arm and the list in her hand, and says nothing at all.

He’s on the porch boards between the two of them, in the Carhartt, with the RAZR in his inside pocket and the onions still on his hands. Down at the curb Lena has the front passenger door open and one boot up on the running board. She looks back up the steps at him, once, and waits.

choices.text: Go see the team come home.

s03a.slug: MONDAY · 2:20 PM · KENNER — THE ROAD OUT OF THE AIRPORT
s03a.music: Kermit Ruffins — “Drop Me Off in New Orleans”
body: The road out of the airport has been a parking lot since breakfast. Both shoulders, five and six deep, as far as Jack can see either way under a high white sky with the wind in it: folding chairs, coolers, pickups backed onto the grass with their tailgates down. The signs are bedsheets, mostly, spray-painted and duct-taped to broom handles. SUPER BOWL CHAMPIONS · WE BEEN WAITING SINCE ’67. Somebody has taped a sheet of this morning’s newspaper over the stop sign at the corner, so the sign says AMEN. A little farther up, on a pillowcase, in house paint: GEAUX HOME. A man is selling Who Dat T-shirts out of a shopping cart, three for twenty, and doing the kind of business Lordstown hasn’t done in a year.

Remy has parked half on the grass and half on what is very likely a fire lane, on the word of a cousin with the parish who said on the phone, “Ain’t a soul writing tickets today, Rem,” and hung up before Remy could get his last name. The plane was due at noon. It’s twenty past two. Not one car has given up its spot.

Half a dozen car radios along this stretch are on OZ, and all of them are playing the same trumpet, a half-second apart, so the song comes down the shoulder in pieces and never quite finishes arriving. Remy has WWL on in the Suburban with all four doors open, where a man has been saying “Wheels down any minute now, folks” for an hour.

Lena goes up the Suburban in three moves: the running board, the hood, a knee on the wipers. Then she’s standing on the roof in Remy’s purple sweatshirt with her hair coming out of its pencil, a hand over her eyes, looking up the road at the terminal. She sits down on the roof rack and holds a hand down to him.

body.text: “You missed the table,” she says. “You’re not missing the roof.”
body.else: She holds the hand there, down past the windshield, until he takes it.

body: He takes it. She pulls harder than she needs to, and he comes up over the hood on his knees, and from the grass Remy yells, “Ohio, that’s a *leased vehicle*.”

They sit at the front of the roof with their legs down over the windshield and their heels on the top of the glass. From up here the road is two banks of people with an empty strip of asphalt down the middle, waiting, and police at the intersection leaning on their motorcycles. It’s cold in the wind. Lena sits on her hands. When that doesn’t work she takes the right one out from under herself and works it in under his thigh instead, against the steel of the rack, and leaves it there, and goes on reading him the signs.

“Since ’66,” she says, of the bedsheet across the road. “Technically. They gave us the team on All Saints’ Day. November the first, nineteen sixty-six. Mémère says forty-three years isn’t anything, for a saint. She says Saint Monica waited seventeen on Augustine and nobody threw *her* a parade.”
“Augustine was the parade.”
“Augustine was the onside kick. Late, and out of nowhere, and everybody in the stands had already given up on him.”
Down at the tailgate Theo has his iPhone out and isn’t doing anything with it but looking at it, and up at the roof, and back at it. He holds it out across the cooler to Kevin, screen down.
“Confiscate it,” Theo says. “I can’t be trusted.”
Kevin takes it and puts it in the inside pocket of his windbreaker and zips the pocket shut.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, “this is worse.”

An old man comes along the shoulder, slow, in a gold windbreaker that has been through a lot of Septembers, with a cardboard sign: TULANE STADIUM 1967 · I WAS THERE. A big man in a Vilma jersey gets up out of his lawn chair and puts the old man in it. Margot is sitting on the hood below Jack’s heels with her knees up and her notebook in her coat, not out of it, and she watches the old man sit down.
“Durkheim,” Margot says. “*Collective effervescence.* A society worshipping itself and calling it a football team.”
Laney turns her head exactly far enough to see the hood and no farther. “Then why are *you* crying?”
Margot wipes under one eye with the side of her thumb and inspects the thumb. “Allergies to the sacred.”

At half past two the RAZR goes against his ribs, in the Carhartt’s inside pocket, and when he gets it out the little screen on the outside of the lid says SKYE (MISFIT). Beside him Lena’s hand comes out from under his leg. She pulls her sleeves down over both hands and holds them in her lap and looks up the road toward the terminal. He opens the phone.

body.text: “Did the man on the porch really cry on a Grand Am,” Skye says, “or is that a metaphor?”
body.else: “Did the man on the porch cry?” Skye says. “Tell me he cried. I took full credit, Jack. I need there to have been crying.”

body: “A green Grand Am. Mississippi plate. The man who owns it cried too.”

“Two grown men and a Pontiac.” She sounds delighted, and her mouth is full. “That’s a two-hander I would *do*. In a parking lot, for tips.” A plastic spoon scrapes a plastic bowl. “It’s lunch. It’s *Monday*. Canada doesn’t know. I’m on the steps of the honey wagon with something they’re calling chili, and there’s a goose. It watched me cross the lot this morning like it had notes.”
“How’s Kyle?”

“Kyle came in this morning in black. I still have his hat, so he found a black cap. He found a black *cap*, Jack. He’s grieving in a palette.” The spoon. “Where are you? It sounds like a county fair.”
“On the roof of a car outside the airport. The team’s plane is two hours late. The parish came.”
“On the *roof*.”
“It’s leased.”

“Good. I hate it when you ruin things you own.” Paper moves on her end, folded and refolded: the sides, out of her coat pocket. “We did Wade this morning. The porch. They flew in a man from Toronto with a very sad beard to be my father, and he’s fine, but the page was lying, so I went to the writer at seven a.m. in a parka. Fifteen years in a truck, and Wade comes up the steps and says *I’m sorry* on page two. Nobody says it on page two. You say it on page forty or you don’t say it. So I got it cut. Now he says ‘Hi, kid,’ and stands there, and Cassie does the rest of the page against a man who won’t apologize. Which was always the scene. They’d just written over it.”

body.text: The paper goes back in the pocket. “I told the beard how you read it in my room. Slow. Like he wasn’t sure he was allowed on the porch.”
body.else: The paper goes back in the pocket. “I told the beard about your pause.”

body: “What’d he do with it?”

“He used it. He’s a professional.” The spoon goes round the bowl. “And I cried. Not the menthol. Second take, right where the truck is, and when they cut, the director came and crouched by the steps in his good scarf and said, ‘Keep that.’ Like I’d brought it from home.”
The spoon stops.
“That’s the problem with being good,” Skye says. “Nobody can tell.”
Up the road a dog is barking at a bedsheet. Jack looks at the toes of his boots on the top of the windshield.
“I could tell,” he says. “In your room. The thermos.”
“You could tell because I let you,” she says, and at the far end of the road, up by the airport, the shoulder starts to yell.

It comes down the road toward them, people getting up out of their chairs in a line like a fuse burning, and Remy is out of the Suburban with both arms up yelling “Wheels down, *wheels down*,” before there’s anything in the sky. Then there is: the jet, lower than seems right, coming in over the roofs of Kenner with its gear hanging and its belly gray against the white, and both banks of the shoulder stand up and cheer at it. They cheer at an airplane. A man on a tailgate holds a baby up to it in both hands.
“What *is* that,” Skye says. “Jack. That’s the same noise.” She’s laughing. “Does that city have one volume?”

He holds the phone up to the sky, as high as his arm goes, until the jet is down behind the trees and the noise has gone after it. When he puts it back to his ear she’s still laughing. It goes out of her, and when she speaks again it’s close to the phone and low.
“Did you think about the picture?”
“Every hour.”
Lena is watching the road where the plane went. Her knee is against his on the roof rack. When he says it, her knee doesn’t go anywhere.

“Good,” Skye says. “Not yet. I’m working up to it.” Somebody across a lot in Burnaby calls a name that isn’t hers, then calls it louder. “That’s me. That’s Cassie. Quick, before they take me: the house. Did anybody go to work?”

“Not one. The man on the porch is home on a Monday for the first time in four years. He was in line at dawn for the paper, and he came back with eight copies and laid them down the table like place cards.”
“Oh, I love him,” Skye says. “Tell him full credit is still pending. I want to see a parade first.”

choices.text: “Love you. Go cry in front of Russ.”
choices.key: On the road out of the airport in Kenner, with the whole road cheering at the team’s plane, you told Skye you love her. Lena was beside you on the roof.
response: “Love you,” he says. “Go cry in front of Russ.”
“Russ is in a parka on a ladder. Russ is very happy for your city.” The name gets called again across the lot. “Love you. Go wave at your team. Bye, Grand Am.”
The hinge shuts. He holds the RAZR closed on his knee. Beside him Lena has her eyes on the road.

The team comes an hour and a half later, when the white over the road has begun to go yellow at the bottom. Police motorcycles first, slow, lights and no sirens; then cars, a long line of them with the windows down and men’s arms out of them slapping hands along the shoulder, and the road goes up the way Dupre Street went up last night, except this travels. Remy, at the edge of the roof, screams himself hoarse at every car, not caring who’s in it. Lena is on her feet on the roof rack with both arms up, and Jack has her by the ankle so the Suburban doesn’t lose her. She looks down at him once. Then back at the road.

choices.text: “The man on the porch would like a word with your Colts fan.”
choices.key: On the road out of the airport in Kenner, Skye called at her lunch. You told her the man on the porch would like a word with her Colts fan.
response: “The man on the porch would like a word with your Colts fan.”
“Kyle’s in hiding,” Skye says. “Kyle has gone to ground. He’s eating his lunch in the van with the goose.” The name again, closer, a man’s voice now. “Coming. *Coming.* Bye, Grand Am.”
He folds the phone shut on her laughing and puts it back inside the Carhartt.

The team comes an hour and a half later: police motorcycles, slow, and then the cars, windows down, men in them slapping every hand on the shoulder, the road going up car by car as the line comes, last night on Dupre Street laid out a mile long. Lena is up on the roof rack with both arms in the air, and Jack has a hand round her ankle so she won’t go over the windshield, and she is yelling at all of them, not caring which car: “Hartley! I’m lighting a candle for your *leg*!”

choices.key: On the road out of the airport in Kenner, Skye called at her lunch. You told her you wish she could see it.
response: “I wish you could see this.”

On her end the generator hums, and the man across the lot gives up calling and starts walking, boots on gravel coming down the line. “Tell me what it looks like,” Skye says. “Later. Tell me slow.” The boots arrive. “Bye, Grand Am.”
The hinge creaks shut. He keeps the phone in his hand on his knee for a while after, with the radios going under him.

The team comes an hour and a half later. Police motorcycles first, their lights going in the dull afternoon; then a caravan of cars with men leaning out of the windows, and a cheer walking along the shoulder beside them at their speed. Remy is hoarse at the roof’s edge. Lena is on her feet with both arms up, and Jack holds her ankle so she won’t go over. When the last car is gone she sits back down beside him on the rack, breathing hard, with her sleeves pushed up past her elbows, and puts her shoulder against his, and they watch the road empty out.

s03g.slug: MONDAY · 1:40 PM · A SUPERMARKET, MID-CITY — MAKING GROCERIES
body: Somebody has decorated the supermarket without deciding between a wake and a wedding: black and gold crepe paper twisted along the tops of the aisles, gold balloons tied to the cart corral with their strings gone slack. The French bread is on a rack by the door in paper sleeves, still warm enough to fog them. In aisle six a stock boy in a Brees jersey kneels by a half-stocked shelf of Zapp’s with a box cutter in his hand, crying. He doesn’t look like he knows why. A woman with a basket has stopped to pat his shoulder anyway. The checkout lady at register two has taped this morning’s front page to the side of her register, AMEN, and every time she rings somebody up she touches it.

Jack pushes. Celeste steers, one hand on the front of the cart and the list in the other, so that mostly he pushes where she points. She reads the list in her whisper, not exactly to him. “Blue Plate. Not the light. The *real* Blue Plate.” Camellia, two pounds. Pickled pork. Crystal. “Bread on the way out. Not now. It gets crushed.”

She knows half the store: two ladies from the parish by the eggs, the butcher, who comes out from behind his glass to hug her with his elbows because his hands are red. She introduces Jack to none of them. Every one of them looks at him, and then at her, and she lets them.

The heavy things turn out to be the big sack of Mahatma off the bottom shelf, which she points at with her chin, and a case of Abita for Tony. While he lifts, she asks him things, and doesn’t wait long for the answers.
“What’s your mama’s name?”
“Maria.”
“What does Maria cook on a Monday?”
“Whatever’s left of Sunday’s gravy.”
“Red gravy?”
He has to think about it. “Red.”
“*Bon*,” Celeste says, in Mémère’s exact up-and-down, and hears herself, and presses her lips together, and reaches for the pickled pork. “She work nights?”
“School office. Days.”
“Days is good. Your daddy go back to the plant?”
“Laid off. Lordstown.”
She nods and puts a second pack of pickled pork in the cart.

In produce she stops at the cantaloupes, which are from Guatemala and too early, and she knows it. She presses the end of one with her thumb and holds it to her face, and puts it back. Her hands are quick and square, the nails cut to nothing. The fourth one goes in the cart.
That’s where Lena finds them, coming through the produce at a run in the purple sweatshirt with her hair still up and the parking lot’s wind in her cheeks.
“The plane’s late,” she says. “Remy’s on the phone with WWL about it. I had him drop me.”
Celeste looks at her over the cart. “Did you.”

“They kept us waiting forty-three years, Mama. They can wait on me one afternoon.” She takes the cart by the handle, her hands between his on the bar for the length of it, and moves him off it with her hip. “You push it like there’s a baby in it.”

From then on she drives. She goes down aisle six past the stock boy and puts a hand on his shoulder on the way — “*Cher*, I know” — and comes back with a bag of Zapp’s, the Voodoo ones, and sets it in Jack’s arms on top of the Abita. A bottle of Crystal of his own, not the one on the list, which she tucks into the crook of his elbow with her fingers in the fold of his sleeve to seat it there. Every one of them is something he has reached for in her mother’s kitchen since Saturday. Up in the ceiling the radio has come round to Ernie K-Doe and “Mother-in-Law.” Celeste looks up at the speaker and keeps her eyes there. Lena gets the Crystal settled.
At the mayonnaise, out of eighteen years of habit, Jack’s free hand goes past the Blue Plate and gets as far as a jar of Miracle Whip.
“Mama,” Lena says.
“I saw.”
“In front of the *Blue Plate*.”
“Ma buys it,” Jack says.
“Your mother is a saint and a Yankee,” Lena says, “and I am praying for her on both counts.” She takes the jar out of his hand and puts it back on the shelf, label out.

The line at register two is eight carts deep, because the whole city skipped work and then remembered at once that it had to eat. When it’s their turn Celeste unloads in the order she wants it bagged, and hums two bars of the song that was on the ceiling ten minutes ago, and stops in the middle of the third. She pays cash out of an envelope. The checkout lady touches AMEN, and counts the change into Jack’s palm instead of Celeste’s.
“Who dat, baby,” she says to him, like she’s been saying it to him for years.

They’re bagged and stacked at the end of the coffee aisle, Lena at the cart, Celeste going down the receipt with a pen, and Jack by a pyramid of Community, red bags and dark tins, with the rice up on his shoulder, when the RAZR goes against his ribs. SKYE (MISFIT), says the little screen on the lid. He’s glad. It comes up in him simple at the sight of the name, and at the end of the aisle Lena’s hands go still on her mother’s cart. He opens the phone where he stands.

body.text: “Did the man on the porch really cry on a Grand Am,” Skye says, “or is that a metaphor?”
body.else: “Did the man on the porch cry?” Skye says. “Tell me he cried. I took full credit, Jack. I need there to have been crying.”

body: “A green one. Mississippi plate. The man who owns it cried too.”

“Two grown men and a Pontiac. I’d do that in a parking lot for tips.” A plastic spoon scrapes a plastic bowl. “It’s lunch. It’s *Monday*. Canada doesn’t know. I’m on the steps of the honey wagon eating something they call chili, and there’s a goose. It watched me cross the lot this morning like it had notes.”
“How’s Kyle?”
“Kyle came in this morning in black. I still have his hat, so he found a black *cap*. He’s grieving in a palette. Where are you? It sounds like a game show with carts.”
“Making groceries.”
“You’re *making* them.”
“It’s what they say here.”

“Oh, that’s good.” Her voice goes up a notch and through the nose: a night manager with a name tag. “Ma’am. Ma’am, I need you to step back from the produce. This young man is *making* a cantaloupe.” And down again. “Whose groceries?”
“The lady of the house. It’s her first day off in four years. I’m the heavy things.”

“You were born to be the heavy things.” Paper rattles on her end, folded and refolded: the sides, out of her coat. “We did Wade this morning. The porch. They flew in a man from Toronto with a very sad beard to be my father, and he’s fine, but the page was lying, so I went to the writer at seven a.m. in a parka. Fifteen years in a truck, and Wade comes up the steps and says *I’m sorry* on page two. Nobody says it on page two. You say it on page forty or you don’t say it. So I got it cut. Now he says ‘Hi, kid,’ and stands there, and Cassie has to do the rest of the page against a man who won’t apologize. Which was always the scene. They’d just written over it.”

body.text: The paper goes back in the pocket. “I told the beard how you read it in my room. Slow. Like he wasn’t sure he was allowed on the porch.”
body.else: The paper goes back in the pocket. “I told the beard about your pause.”

body: “What’d he do with it?”

“He used it. He’s a professional.” The spoon goes round the bowl. “And I cried. Not the menthol. Second take, right where the truck is, and when they cut, the director came and crouched by the steps in his good scarf and said, ‘Keep that.’ Like I’d brought it from home.”
“That’s the problem with being good,” Skye says. “Nobody can tell.”
Jack looks at the tins along the bottom of the pyramid. “I could tell. In your room. Where it quit.”
“You could tell because I let you,” she says, and over Jack’s head the ceiling cuts the boudin off in the middle of a word.

A click, a hum, and a man on WWL, very fast, turned up all the way by somebody in the office: “— wheels are *down*, folks, they are on the ground in Kenner —” The store stops. A checker at register four puts her arms up with a can of Ro-Tel in one hand. A woman lifts her baby out of the cart seat toward the speaker, and everybody in the place cheers at the ceiling, the stock boy loudest, from aisle six, still on his knees.
“What *is* that,” Skye says. “Jack. That’s the same noise.” She’s laughing. “Does that city have one volume?”
He holds the phone up to the speaker until the man on WWL has said it three more ways. When he brings it down the laugh has gone out of her, and she’s close to the phone, and low.
“Did you think about the picture?”
“Every hour.”

At the end of the aisle Lena takes a can of the chicory off the bottom of the pyramid and puts it in the cart, on top of the paid-for bags, without looking at it. Celeste’s eyes go from her daughter to Jack and back to the coffee. She lifts the can out of the cart and sets it back where it came from, and goes on down the receipt with her pen.

“Good,” Skye says. “Not yet. I’m working up to it.” Across a lot in Burnaby somebody calls a name that isn’t hers, and then calls it louder. “That’s me. That’s Cassie. Quick, before they take me: did anybody in that city go to work?”
“Not the man on the porch. A kid in here is crying on the potato chips.”
“Your city cries on things. It’s a motif.” The bowl scrapes up off the step. “Tell the man on the porch full credit is still pending. I want to see a parade first.”

response: “Love you,” he says. “Go cry in front of Russ.”
“Russ is up a ladder in a parka. Russ is very happy for your city.” The name again, nearer, and boots on gravel coming down the line of trailers. “Love you. Go carry something heavy. Bye, Grand Am.”

The hinge shuts. He puts the RAZR back inside the Carhartt and settles the rice. At the end of the aisle Lena has turned the cart toward the doors and stands at the handle with her back to him, and her mother is still on the receipt.

“Rice,” Celeste says, in the same whisper she started the list in, and makes a mark. “Camellia, two pounds. Pickled pork, *two*.” She takes the change off Jack’s palm and folds it into the envelope with the receipt. “Bread now, baby.”

choices.key: By the coffee in a Mid-City supermarket, Skye called at her lunch. You told her the man on the porch would like a word with her Colts fan.
response: “The man on the porch would like a word with your Colts fan.”

“Kyle’s in hiding,” Skye says. “Kyle has gone to ground. He’s eating his chili in a van with the windows up and the goose looking in.” The name again, a man’s voice now, closer. “Coming. *Coming.* Bye, Grand Am.”
He folds the phone shut on her laughing. At the cart Lena is reading the back of a bag of Zapp’s with the attention she usually saves for Saint Paul.
“Blue Plate,” Celeste tells the receipt, and makes her mark. “The *real*. Crystal, two.” Her pen stops on the second one. “One’s his.” She doesn’t look up. “Lena. The bread.”

choices.key: By the coffee in a Mid-City supermarket, Skye called at her lunch. You told her you wish she could see it.
response: “I wish you could see this.”

A generator hums on her end, and the man across the lot gives up calling and starts walking, boots on gravel. “Tell me what it looks like,” Skye says. “Later. Tell me slow.” The boots arrive. “Bye, Grand Am.”

The hinge creaks shut. He stands with it closed in his hand and the rice on his shoulder while the ceiling clicks back to the oldies in the middle of somebody’s chorus, and down the aisle Lena rolls the cart toward the doors and back again.

“Zapp’s,” Celeste says, and marks it. “Barq’s. Abita, one case, for your daddy, and I don’t want to hear about it.” She folds the receipt into her purse and looks at the two of them, her daughter at the cart and Jack by the coffee, both of them waiting on her. “Bread, babies.”

s04.slug: MONDAY · 6:05 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT STEPS — WHAT IT COSTS

body.text: They get back from Kenner with the sky going and his ears still ringing. Remy yelled the last of his voice at a caravan on the airport road and has talked since by horn, two short taps at every corner, and every corner taps back. At the curb he gives the house one long one.
body.else: The groceries went up the steep front steps at three, two bags at a time, with Celeste in the door counting them in under her breath, and when the count came out right she took the last two off his arms herself. “Sit, baby. You carried.” He has been sitting, more or less, ever since: an hour asleep in the attic with his boots on, and now the front step.

body: Dupre Street has gone back to being a street. Three houses up, a man in a Saints windbreaker is hosing WHO DAT off the back glass of his Buick, and the white shoe polish runs down over the bumper and along the gutter toward the corner. The porch across the way has a cooler on it and a folding chair and, for the first time since Saturday, nobody. The last of the light has gone amber over the roofs. Jack sits on the top step with his forearms on his knees, and the RAZR goes off in the Carhartt’s inside pocket against his ribs.
The little screen on the lid says ANCHOR. Out there it’s the dead hour between the lunch counter and the supper one, when Gloria does the pies.

“We watched it at the counter,” Gloria says, instead of hello. “Me and Rudy. Merle came in at the half and sat through the rest with a cup of coffee and let it go cold. Rudy cried.” Somewhere behind her a sheet pan goes into the rack. “Don’t tell him I told you.”
“When?”

“The interception. He had his rosary out on the ticket rail, and when the boy went down the sideline he put a bar towel over his whole head and kept it there through the extra point. He says in Soledad you were Saints or you were Raiders, and he wasn’t going to be a Raider.”
“I won’t tell him.”
“Tell him you heard. Leave me out of it.”

body.text: “Did the grandmother eat it?”
body.else: “Did they eat the pie?”

body.text: “Saturday night,” Jack says. “Off a fork, standing up in the kitchen. She said *Bon*.”
body.else: “Every crumb,” Jack says. “The grandmother had the last of it off a fork, standing up.”

body.text: Out in Marisol the register drawer runs out and bumps shut. “Well,” Gloria says. And then, to whatever pie is in front of her: “Pecan keeps. People don’t know that about pecan.”
body.else: Out in Marisol the register drawer runs out and bumps shut. “Well,” Gloria says.

body: “Now business.” The grease pencil, Jack would bet money, has come out of her hair. “Hector’s faster than you on the Hobart, hon, and he’s got a baby, and he wants your Saturdays.”

Thursday went to Hector before Christmas, for the baby, and Hector has had the rest of his shifts since Friday. Saturday is the shift with the fishermen in it, seven to one, and the fishermen pay in cash and tip in it. Up the street the man has turned his hose off and stands looking at his clean back glass.
“I told him Saturdays are spoken for,” Gloria says. “Come back the twentieth and earn them.”

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’ Thursday I asked her for Saturday night. ‘Who’s she?’ ‘You met her.’ ‘Boysenberry.’ She gave it to Rudy’s nephew. Her granddaughter got her watching *Sweetwater*; Thursdays at nine, for the clothes. She rated Cassidy a vanilla custard. Skye agreed. Thursday I asked her for the trip. Theo asked her Tuesday; she told him it wasn’t his to ask. Hector has my shifts — the baby’s six weeks. She counted my tips out early into an envelope with my name on it in grease pencil. Hale told her about the dog. In front of the dog. She made me pick the pie for the Broussards. Sunday’s game, Monday’s dead hour: she told me she and Rudy watched it at the counter, and Rudy cried. Hector wants my Saturdays. She told him they’re spoken for. Come back the twentieth and earn them.

choices.key: From the Broussards’ steps you called Gloria’s Saturdays a gift and thanked her. Don’t thank me, she said. Come back.
response: “Thank you, Gloria.”
“Don’t thank me. Come back.” Behind her the Hobart starts into its cycle, and she hangs up on it.
He sits with the shut phone on his knee. Up the street the Buick drips into the gutter, and its back glass is only glass again.

choices.text: “Give him the Saturdays if the baby needs them.”
choices.key: From the Broussards’ steps you told Gloria to give Hector your Saturdays, for the baby. The dumbest thing you ever said to her, she said. She’s keeping it.
response: “Give him the Saturdays,” Jack says, “if the baby needs them.”
“That’s the dumbest thing you ever said to me.” A pause long enough for the Hobart to cycle behind her. “I’m keeping it.”
“Gloria —”

“You’ve still got Tuesdays. And whatever I feel like.” The line clicks over to the dial tone. He does the sum on the step, the one he knew the answer to before he said it, and puts the phone back inside his coat.

choices.text: “Hector can have the Hobart. I want the fishermen.”
choices.key: From the Broussards’ steps you told Gloria that Hector could have the Hobart; you wanted the fishermen. Everybody does, she said. Your Saturdays are waiting.
response: “Hector can have the Hobart,” Jack says. “I want the fishermen.”
“Everybody wants the fishermen, hon. That’s why they’re Saturdays.” Something slides onto the pass on her end, and somebody hits the bell. “The twentieth. Don’t make me hold a door.”

s04a.slug: MONDAY · 6:25 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH — NOTHING ABOUT FOOTBALL
body: By the time the streetlight at the corner comes on he has moved to the swing, which takes his weight with one complaint from the chains and settles. The screen door opens behind him, and it’s Theo, in a gray cashmere sweater with the sleeves shoved up, carrying his MacBook open in both hands like a tray.
“Your Englishman wrote,” Theo says. “You never logged out Sunday, and I have no character.” He sets the laptop on Jack’s knees, screen up, already open to it. “I’m not here.”
He isn’t. He’s back inside before the swing has stopped moving, and from somewhere past the front room Laney says something to him, low, and he says something back, lower.

Seminar met. The Moviegoer, in the absence of its two most motivated readers. Mr. Hargrove argued both of your positions and lost to himself. Mr. Noorzai asked whether you would be back. I said the Saints had won and that this was not a theological event.

Four thousand words each, the Monday you return. Nothing about football.

—A.H.

body: Hale’s own *Moviegoer*, with Hale’s pencil arguing in all its margins, is upstairs in the duffel under Remy’s Tiger. Jack is still on Mr. Noorzai when the screen door goes again.

It’s Lena, in her socks, with her sleeves pushed up past her elbows and her LG open in her hand. She doesn’t come to the swing. She sits down on the top step with her back to the porch post and her feet two steps down, facing the street, and reads off her little screen in vowels that are trying very hard to be from Oxford and are mostly from Mid-City: “‘*Nothing about football.*’”

body.text: Beside her on the step stands the mailing tube, Celeste’s tape round both ends and FRANK COSTIGAN · GLENWOOD AVE across it in Tony’s capitals, ready for whatever day the post office decides this city is going back to work.

body: “He wrote you too,” Jack says.
“He wrote *us*.” She scrolls with her thumb. “‘Its two most motivated readers.’ Read that fast and it’s an insult. Read it slow and it’s a compliment. He’s going to deny both.”
“Caleb argued both our positions.”

“And lost to himself.” She lays her head back against the post. “Poor Caleb. He’d have been so proud of himself right up till the last ten minutes.” She scrolls back to the top. “They read Binx without us. In Hollis 302, with the radiator going. A book about a boy from Gentilly who goes to the movies all the way through Carnival so he doesn’t have to be anywhere.” She points the LG up Dupre Street, past the Odyssey and the dripping Buick, toward the dark coming in off the lake. “Gentilly’s right over there.”
“You grew up with boys who think they’re in it.”
She turns her head and looks at him, on the swing, with the laptop on his knees and Hale’s sentences lit up on it. “I did,” she says. “Half of them will be on Canal tomorrow.”
The cursor waits in the reply.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the first quarter of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus. The Conversion of St. Paul: he did Saul for Caleb. He’s in New York Thursday, being rude to a churchman on a stage, so Greene moved to his house Wednesday with the State of the Union on — phones in the dog’s bowl, bring a guest, sides assigned: me for Sarah’s silence, Lena against. Opposite ends of a door. He turned the President off before the rebuttal. When Lena and I went at each other across his table he stood up and stopped it, in a voice I’ve never heard out of him, and he wasn’t amused. Berkeley felt it through the floor. On the deck he said the table was his. He asked where a Catholic goes at eight on a Wednesday. Give him my regards. He blessed my dog. He may like to do it again. Monday he gave us Joyce, “The Dead,” and taught it as if Wednesday never happened, and everybody at the table knew what it was for. He kept Lena after with the door shut. Then me: until Wednesday no argument at his table had ever sent the dog under the kitchen table. He said I went for the places that hurt, that I’m good at it, and that he’d rather I weren’t. Miss Ivors left before the goose. Nobody remembers what she was right about. Thursday he canceled the seminar for a lecture in Berkeley and gave me the week. Go. Write me something about it. Four thousand words on the second line, not one of them *liminal* — Theo’s terms; he took them. He lent me his own *Moviegoer*, his pencil in the margins. It ends on Ash Wednesday. Thirty hours in a van: he’d like to be the luggage. Monday he wrote to the two of us and nobody else: the seminar met on *The Moviegoer* without us, and Caleb argued both our sides and lost to himself. Four thousand words each, the Monday we’re back. Nothing about football. He noticed both replies came from the same city.
