He comes down to the step with the laptop and sits beside her, and the MacBook’s corner digs the RAZR into his ribs until he lays it on the boards by hers, face-up. At the curb the Odyssey’s lipstick 0 has gone dark.

s05.slug: MONDAY · 7:40 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN TABLE — RED BEANS
body: The kitchen table seats eight, so Tony has put the card table on the end of it, and the leaf in, and a bedsheet over the seam where the two don’t meet, and around it on dining chairs and folding chairs and the piano bench from the front room and an upturned five-gallon bucket that Remy says is his by right sit fifteen people and a baby. Outside, Dupre Street has gone dark. The bulb over the table makes a yellow room inside the yellow room.

The pot has been on since noon. Somewhere in it, gone to nothing, are the onions he cut, and the pickled pork has given everything it had to the beans, and the rice steams in Mémère’s big colander by the stove. Under Clovis’s chair at the corner Aints III lies with his chin on his paws and his bandana on, waiting on the law of averages. The Magic Chef ticks as it cools.

At Celeste’s elbow there’s a Tupperware filled to the lid, with LUC on a strip of masking tape across the top. “Sixteen hours,” she says, when Jack looks at it. “He’s dead to the world. He’ll eat it at one in the morning, like a raccoon.”
Tony points at Kevin.

Kevin has been pointed at before. He puts his fork down and bows his head and says it short and in English, from *Bless us, O Lord* to *through Christ our Lord, amen*, and then, with every spoon at the table already lifted: “And thank You for the Saints.”
“*Amen*,” says Mémère, to the Saints, and crosses herself a second time.

Josie is aggrieved: a full day of school on the Monday after the Super Bowl, in this city, and early dismissal tomorrow. “On the *day of the parade*,” Josie says, for the third time since three o’clock. “Like it’s a favor. Like somebody sat up nights thinking of it.”
“It is a favor,” says Celeste.
Jude, beside her, eats his rice off the back of his fork. Jack hasn’t had a word out of him since Saturday.

Across Lucille’s head, Beau passes him the hot sauce without being asked. Beau is Tess’s husband, an Entergy lineman with a sunburn in February and the stillness of somebody who has spent eighteen hours in a bucket truck getting the power right along tomorrow’s route. He has been saving his words since he sat down.
“Youngstown,” Beau says. “Your daddy GM?”
“Lordstown.”
“What line?”
“Cobalt.”
Beau nods, the way men nod at a model year. “They bring him back?”
“Not yet.”
Beau nods again and hands him the rice. Pop would like Beau. Pop would ask him about his truck.
At the head of the table Tony puts his spoon down and stands, which in this family means legislation.
“Every Fat Tuesday since nineteen eighty-one,” Tony says, “this family goes out as one thing.”
“Crawfish, the first year,” Remy tells Jack, as a public service. “The year after the Pope came, the Swiss Guard. The year after the water, blue tarps. Last year —”
“And this year,” says Tony.
“The bag,” says Remy.
The table splits down the middle like a union hall on a contract vote.
“We can’t wear the *bag*,” says Josie. “We *won*.”
“That’s the *point*, Jo,” says Tess, from behind the baby.
“I still got mine,” says Clovis, with his mouth full.
Celeste says Tony’s name in a whisper that stops the kitchen as well as any shout would, and Tony stays standing.

body.text: Jack has heard this one. On the porch at halftime, with the transistor on the rail: nineteen-eighty, one and fifteen, a Schwegmann’s sack for a dollar, and a girl of twenty with her sewing scissors in her purse, cutting him the eyeholes in the parking lot. The girl is at the other end of the table, passing the French bread.
body.else: “In nineteen-eighty,” Remy tells Jack, “we lost every game, so Daddy wore a grocery sack on his head to the Dome, and Mama cut the holes with a steak knife.”

body.text: “We won one,” Tony says. “And it was her sewing scissors. Get it right or get out of my kitchen.”

body: “Wear it for penance,” Lena says. She has her elbows on the oilcloth and her spoon pointed at her father. “You don’t take off the sackcloth because the siege lifted. You keep it on to remember what it cost.”
“Wear it for Easter,” Jack says. “Easter isn’t Good Friday with better lighting. He came back with the holes still in Him, and He told Thomas to put his hand in them. Same wounds. Different Sunday.”
“*Ohio’s* right,” Remy says, and hits the table. “It’s Easter. We’re *Easter* now.”
Lena puts her spoon down. She looks at her brother, and at Jack, and at her brother again, and pushes her sleeves the rest of the way up.
“Oh,” she says. “Magdalena is *going* to say something.”
“Lord,” Celeste whispers.

“Nineveh,” Lena says. “Jonah, chapter three. Forty days and the city’s destroyed, and the king hears it, and he gets up off his throne and takes off his robe and puts on sackcloth and sits down in the ashes. And then he makes a *decree*. Man and beast, Remy. *Man and beast.* Not a bite, not a sip, everybody in sackcloth, the cattle too, the sheep too, cows in sackcloth in the street crying out to God. And God sees it, and He relents, and the city is spared.” She picks the spoon back up. “And nowhere in that book does anybody take it off the cows. Go read the end. The last word of the book of Jonah is *cattle*. God gets the last word and He spends it on the livestock, saved, still in their sackcloth. You don’t take it off. You wear it to the parade.”
Remy opens his mouth, and shuts it, and puts both hands up. “Okay. The cows.”

At the far end of the table Mémère says something in French, short and dry, with her spoon in the air, and Celeste puts her hand over her mouth and keeps it there, and Lena goes red to the ears. Jack doesn’t have the French for it, and nobody gives it to him.

Under the table a stocking foot finds his boot. It comes from across the corner, where Lena sits, and settles against the side of it with the toes over his laces, warm through the leather, while she eats her beans as if she has never in her life had feet. He doesn’t move the boot. He eats his beans, and they are very good, and he couldn’t tell anybody one thing about them. At the next corner Josie has developed an interest in the ceiling fan. Across the table Theo is asking Clovis about dogs with a concentration Clovis has never had from anybody.
“*Assez*,” says Mémère.

Tony is still standing. “It’s a *bag*,” he tells all of them. He reaches back and opens the drawer by the stove, and Celeste reaches past him into it without looking and comes out with a pair of black-handled sewing scissors as long as her hand and holds them up under the bulb, and the kitchen applauds them. Remy whistles through his fingers. Clovis bangs the table with his palm.

“Same scissors,” Tony says. “Gold paint. A sack from the store. Eyeholes.” He looks down the table at every one of them, his mother and his wife and his children, and the baby, and the five from California. “We wore it in shame,” Tony says. “We’ll wear it in glory.”

Celeste is already up. She takes a marker out of the drawer and a stack of brown paper sacks off the top of the refrigerator and goes round the table behind the chairs, a hand on each shoulder as she passes and her sizes in a whisper, like a ward round at six in the morning.
“Remy, medium. Tess, medium. Beau, medium, I don’t care what you say. Twins, small.”
“*Mama*,” says Josie.
“Small, baby. Lucille’s in my arms; she’s a bag already. Mémère wears her veil.” There’s no arguing with that. “Laney. My redhead gets sequins.”
Laney puts a hand to her heart. “*Gold* sequins, Mrs. Broussard?”
“Is there another kind?”
Theo looks up from Clovis and the dogs. “Am I a bag?”
“Everybody’s a bag, baby.”
Margot sets her spoon down. “I’ll attend as a bag.”
“Kevin, medium.”
“I’m a medium in most things, ma’am,” Kevin says.
“Clovis brings his own.”
Clovis lifts his glass to that, and Aints III sneezes under the chair.
“Lena, medium.”
“I’m a *small*, Mama.”
“You’re a medium, and you’ll thank me on Fat Tuesday. Tony, extra large, and he knows why.”
From the far end, Mémère: “*Et Luc?*”
“Luc’s a large,” Celeste says. “He’ll find his at one in the morning with his beans.”
She comes round behind Jack’s chair last. She uncaps the marker and writes on a sack against the back of the chair, in capitals, without asking him one thing.
“Baby,” Celeste says, “you’re a large.”
He has not been asked. Down the table, everybody finds their spoon.

journal.title: Celeste Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s mother. A nurse — she came to the door in scrubs. Gives her orders in a whisper. Saturday night she was in the door when I came up her steps with Lena asleep, and she didn’t ask me one thing. Sunday she ran eleven people through one bathroom in a whisper. Ice, baby. In the street after the game, with the whole city yelling, she said to me: Bring them home, baby. Monday she took a personal day, her first since the storm, and made groceries. At red beans she sized the whole table for the bag in a whisper. Baby, you’re a large.

choices.key: At Monday red beans Mrs. Broussard sized the whole table for the family’s Mardi Gras bag. You’re a large, she said. You said you’d be honored.
response: “I’d be honored, Mrs. Broussard.”
“You’d be a large,” says Celeste.
Tony, to his beans: “He’d be *honored*.”
“*Antoine*,” says Mémère.
Celeste sets the sack down on the oilcloth at Jack’s plate, LARGE side up, square to the edge of the table, and goes to put the scissors back.

choices.text: “In Youngstown we wear the bag all year.”
choices.key: At Monday red beans Mrs. Broussard sized the whole table for the family’s Mardi Gras bag. You’re a large. You told the table that in Youngstown you wear the bag all year.
response: “In Youngstown,” Jack says, “we wear the bag all year.”

Tony laughs until he has to put his spoon down. He laughs with his eyes shut and a hand on his chest, and Mémère says “*Antoine*,” and he laughs anyway, and Clovis catches it off him, and Aints III comes out from under the chair to see what he’s missing.
Celeste pats the sack down at Jack’s plate, LARGE side up, and lets the table laugh itself out.

choices.key: At Monday red beans Mrs. Broussard sized you for the family’s bag. You said, plainly, that you’re not family. Only Lena heard it.
response: “I’m not family, ma’am,” Jack says.

He says it at an ordinary volume into a kitchen with fifteen people in it, and it goes nowhere. Remy is asking for the hot sauce. Mémère is telling Josie something in French with a finger up. Tess is wiping Lucille’s chin with the corner of a dish towel. Celeste is already writing LARGE.
Across the corner of the table Lena looks at her plate. Under the table her foot doesn’t move off his boot.
Celeste puts the sack at his plate and the scissors back in the drawer.

s05a.slug: MONDAY · 8:40 PM · THE KITCHEN — THE DISHES
body: Lena washes. He dries. Celeste has gone to sit down for the first time since she got up, and the kitchen has emptied round the two of them into the front room, where the television is on with the sound off and Mémère is in her chair under the lamp.

The house is a shotgun, every door in a line, and from the drainboard Jack can see straight down it to the front room: Theo and Laney on the couch, side by side, with the television on mute, and every so often Laney reaches over without a word and takes hold of Theo’s wrist, hard, like a woman on an airplane in weather. At the deep sink by the back door Kevin is rinsing a spoon. He has been rinsing it for some time.
When Lena opens the refrigerator to put the butter away, the Tupperware is on the second shelf with LUC across the lid, waiting for one in the morning.

She hands him the plates by the rim. Every plate, the edge of it pinched between her finger and thumb, held out at the length of her arm so that his hand can come in from the other side and their hands won’t meet. They meet anyway. They meet on the third plate and on the fifth, and on the gravy boat, which has a handle, and she hands him that by the lip, so that the side of her wet thumb goes along his knuckles and away. Each time it takes everything he has to think about the towel. He dries the gravy boat for a long time.
From her chair in the front room, Mémère: “*Magdalena.* The pot.”
“I *know* the pot.”

The pot is Mémère’s big black one, sitting on the back of the stove with the last of the beans gone hard round the inside of it. Lena runs the tap into it. Then she flicks the water off her fingers at him, sideways, and doesn’t look to see if it landed. It lands on his cheek, cold, and he dries that too.

The dish rack fills. The window over the sink is black, and the bulb has put the two of them in it, side by side, her sleeves up and the towel over his shoulder, and the table behind them, and on the oilcloth at his place the paper sack with LARGE on it in Celeste’s capitals, standing up on its own.

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 11:50 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — GOLD PAINT
body: The cold came down in the night. At seven Jack said the penance on his knees at the attic window, with the glass gone gray in front of him and the wind worrying the tin on the shed roof. He got through it clean, start to finish, without going back for a single word, and he doesn’t trust it. By noon the porch boards are dark with a wet that came from no rain he heard fall, Tony and Clovis have been gone since six with two folding chairs to hold a corner on Canal, and down Celeste’s counter seven thermoses stand in a row with their caps screwed on, six steel ones and a plaid one from some other decade, each with a strip of masking tape and her handwriting on it.
“Six bags of coffee and one of milk,” Celeste says, and smooths the last strip of tape down with her thumb. “Nobody drinks the milk.”

The twins come in the back door at a run at ten to twelve with their school bags still on their backs, let out early for the parade, and Josie announces it from the doormat to the whole house, and Mémère, from the daybed, says something back in French about the floor.

body.text: In three days Jude Broussard has said *yes sir* to Jack, and *no*, and nothing else. He comes down the table now with his bag still on and sets a box on the oilcloth by Jack’s coffee: a green plastic dinosaur behind a cellophane window, BRONTOSAURUS EXCELSUS on the end in gift-shop lettering, last seen on Saturday night in the duffel at the foot of the attic ladder. The box is in better shape than when it left Cabazon. Jude puts one finger on the name.
“They took the name away,” he says. “It’s *Apatosaurus* now.”
“My sister’s eight,” Jack says. “Don’t tell her.”
Jude looks at the box, and at Jack, and at the box. “Okay,” he says, and picks it up again and carries it off up the hall toward the ladder under his arm, with the school bag bumping on his back.

In three days Jude Broussard has said *yes sir* to Jack, and *no*, and nothing else. He sits down across the table with his bag still on and watches Jack eat a cold biscuit, every bite of it, without blinking, and when it’s gone he says, “Does Ohio have dinosaurs?”
“Trilobites,” Jack says. “It’s the state fossil.”
Jude thinks about that for some time. “Okay.”

body: Lena has the end of the table by the window, where the light is, such as it is today. She has Tess’s good makeup brush, borrowed out of the bathroom while Tess is in the front room feeding the baby, and a pot of gold face paint from the drugstore on Carrollton, and a saucer, and a wet rag over her shoulder, and she paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Josie sits for hers with her chin up and her eyes on the ceiling. Lena lays it on in three strokes, the middle petal and then the two that curl away from it, and the band across, steady as a man running a bead down a seam, and sits back to look.
“Bigger than Jude’s,” Josie says.
“Hush. You’re a saint in a window, not the foreman.” Lena rinses the brush in the saucer. “Jude. Here.”

Jude flinches at the touch of the brush. “Hold still, *cher*,” Lena tells him, “or you get a crawfish,” and he holds, and gets his, and gets the rag across his eyebrow where the second curl went wrong.
Then she holds the brush out across the corner of the table at Jack, with gold on the end of it.
He reaches for it. She takes it back out of his reach and leans over the corner of the table instead, and takes his jaw in her hand, and turns his face to the window, to what light there is.

The brush is cold and wet and very light. She does the middle petal first, up the bone under his eye, and her breath is on the paint to keep it from running, warm, and smelling of chicory. Her hand is under his chin. Her eyes are on her own work and nowhere else, with the line between her brows that she gets over a page of Aquinas, and her thumb is at the corner of his mouth, holding the skin where she wants it. He wants, very simply, to turn his face the last little way into her palm. He keeps it where she put it.

The back door bangs open. Tony is in it with the transistor in one hand, back from Canal for the thermoses, red in the face from the wind, and he takes in his kitchen table at a glance. “Don’t you paint the Ohio boy —”
She has already done the first curl.
At the stove, eating cold red beans out of the pot with a serving spoon, Remy says, “*Brother-in-law.*”

journal.title: Jude Broussard
journal.text: Josie’s twin. Doesn’t talk, and then does. Found Rosie’s dinosaur in my duffel and kept it safe three days. They took the name away, he says. It’s *Apatosaurus* now. He won’t tell her.

journal.title: Jude Broussard
journal.text: Josie’s twin. Doesn’t talk, and then does. His first question for me was whether Ohio has dinosaurs.

choices.key: Tuesday in the kitchen Lena painted a fleur-de-lis on your face. You held still. It took longer than a fleur-de-lis needs.
response: He holds still. It takes longer than a fleur-de-lis needs. She does the second curl, and the band across, and goes back over the first curl, fine as it was, and the band again; she wipes a fleck off his cheekbone with the corner of the rag from somewhere he couldn’t see it; and the whole time Tony stands in the back door with the transistor going and the cold coming in round him, and doesn’t shut it. When she’s done she blows on the paint to dry it and gives him back his face.
Celeste is in the hall door with a thermos in the crook of each arm and the rest in the milk crate at her feet. “Coats. All of you. It’s February on Canal.”

choices.key: Tuesday in the kitchen Lena painted a fleur-de-lis on your face, and, at your request, a very small Browns helmet beside it. There. Now you’re both.
response: “Make it a Browns helmet,” he says, out of the side of his mouth she isn’t holding.

She doesn’t answer him. She lets go of his face, takes Josie’s red lipstick off the windowsill, dabs it on the saucer, works the gold into it with the end of the brush until it comes up orange, and takes his face back. Beside the fleur-de-lis, up toward his ear, she paints a very small, very accurate orange helmet with a stripe down the middle and no logo on the side, because there isn’t one.
“There,” she says. “Now you’re both.”
Josie gets up on her knees on her chair to see. “That’s *sad*.”

choices.key: Tuesday in the kitchen Lena painted a fleur-de-lis on your face, and you took the brush and painted hers. The whole kitchen watched. In the doorway Laney shut her eyes.
response: He takes the brush out of her fingers. She lets him. She sits back in her chair and turns her own face to the window for him, chin up, and shuts her eyes.

He is no painter. The middle petal goes on fat, the curls go on like two hooks off an overhead crane, and his hand isn’t as steady at her cheekbone as he would like. The kitchen has gone quiet round the two of them: Tony with the radio in the back door, Remy with the spoon halfway to his mouth, Josie on her knees on her chair. In the hall doorway Laney, in Remy’s old Saints parka, stops dead, looks, pulls the hood up over her hair with both hands, and shuts her eyes, lips going, like a woman at a novena.
Lena opens her eyes and finds herself in the dark of the window glass. “It’s a crawfish,” she says.
“It’s a fleur-de-lis.”
“It’s a crawfish, and I’m wearing it.”

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 2:30 PM → 4:45 PM · CANAL STREET — THE WAIT
s07.music: The Soul Rebels — “Let Your Mind Be Free”
body: Tony’s corner on Canal is twenty feet of curb, a strip of dead winter grass on the neutral ground behind it, and a length of streetcar track that a man in a reflective vest has asked him twice, politely, not to put a chair on. Tony has stood somewhere on Canal Street for every big thing in this city since 1981. He picked this piece of it at six o’clock this morning in the dark, with his brother Clovis and two folding chairs, and he hasn’t given up a foot of it since.

The floats aren’t due on Canal until after dark, and at half past two the crowd is already here. It has been here since breakfast: ten deep along the curb and on the neutral ground behind it, both sides of the street, as far up toward the Dome and down toward the river as Jack can see. Stepladders stand along the curb with plywood seats bolted across their tops, a kid on every one already and a parent holding the legs. A man in a blue Colts jersey with MANNING across the back is being forgiven, loudly, by strangers. “He’s from *here*, baby,” a woman in a gold wig tells him, and kisses him on the cheek, and the man in the jersey stands there and takes it with his eyes shut.

The Broussards have the corner furnished. Clovis is in one folding chair with Aints III sitting between his boots in a quilted dog coat with a fleur-de-lis sewn on the back. Tess is in the other with Lucille in her lap, zipped into a black-and-gold snowsuit with the hood up, so that the baby looks out at the parade route like a very small astronaut who has landed somewhere unexpected and has questions. Beau is up a ladder, because Beau climbs poles for Entergy and trusts a ladder more than he trusts the ground. Clovis’s pickup is pulled up on the grass behind them with the tailgate down. Celeste has the thermoses in a milk crate at her feet, and a sleeve of foam cups. Mémère stayed home with Channel 4.
“She told me, ‘I saw nineteen-eighty in person,’” Celeste says, pouring. “‘I can see this on the television.’”

Down the block, at the corner, NOPD has a line of barricades out, and Luc is on one of them in uniform with his hands on the rail and his eyes on the crowd. He doesn’t look over at his family. A little after three he does, a single time: across Canal, over all those heads, a nod. After that it’s the crowd again.

Tony stands at the curb with his hands on his hips and looks up Canal and down it, at his city out on its own sidewalks on a Tuesday afternoon with the stores shut. “Biggest crowd this city ever had,” he says, to anybody.
A man on the next ladder says, “Amen.”

Behind them on the neutral ground a brass band is warming up, a sousaphone trying the same three notes over and over, two trumpets talking over each other. Then they fall into the same song together, and the people on the grass around them start to move.

It’s gray. It has been gray since dawn, a low lid of cloud over the city, and the wind comes down Canal off the river and finds every gap in everybody. Lena is in Remy’s purple sweatshirt with a jean jacket over it that might have been warm in October. She has been running the corner for an hour. She moved a man’s cooler out from in front of Lucille without consulting the man; she told Jack where to stand, and then where to stand instead. She is also shaking.
“You’re cold,” he says.
“I’m *excited*. It’s a parade.”
“This isn’t cold.”

“It’s cold, and it’s wet, and the wind’s off the river.” Her teeth are going. “Your Yankee cold is dry, and you brag on it like a virtue. This is a damp, low-lying, Catholic cold. It gets in the bones and says a novena there.”
He takes the Browns knit off his own head, the Glenwood spare, orange with the brown band, and pulls it down over her hair to her eyebrows.
Tony, from the curb: “Take that off my daughter’s head.”
“It’s warm, Daddy.”

Tony looks at her in it. He opens his mouth and shuts it, and takes the matter up with the sky over Canal instead, at length, without a word, and on the neutral ground behind him Remy, with a go-cup of his own, crosses himself.

An hour in, with the band on its third song and the wind no better, she turns round from the street, sizes up his open coat, and steps inside it. Back to his chest. Her shoulders under his collarbones, the knit under his chin. He closes the Carhartt round both of them and it nearly goes: he gets three of the buttons done up over the front of her and holds the rest of it shut with his arms crossed over her.
“It’s forty degrees, Youngstown,” she says, facing the street. “Don’t flatter yourself.”

He doesn’t. He stands there with her. She’s warm all down the front of him and cold at the edges, where the wind gets in at the hem, and the knit under his chin smells of his own head and her shampoo, and her hands come up out of the sweatshirt sleeves and take hold of his wrists where they cross over her. He can feel every breath she takes go out against his arms. He stands like this. Over her head the band goes into something slower, and a man in front of them lifts his little girl onto his shoulders, and at the curb Tony keeps his back to the two of them and his face to the street.

Twenty feet up the curb, on purpose, Theo and Laney stand shoulder to shoulder with their backs to the corner and their faces to the street. They have been standing like that for the better part of an hour, and they haven’t turned round.

body.text: At the tailgate Theo has his iPhone out and is doing nothing with it but looking at it, and over toward the corner, and back at it. He holds it out to Kevin across a bag of Zapp’s, screen down.
“Confiscate it,” Theo says. “I can’t be trusted.”
Kevin takes it and zips it into the inside pocket of his windbreaker. When Laney looks round at the two of them, Kevin says, “I’m holding it. I’m not agreeing to it.”

A city garbage truck comes down Canal ahead of everything, slow, clearing the route, with two men riding the back step in orange vests, and the crowd cheers it the length of the block. The men on the step take their gloves off and bow. Margot, on the tailgate beside Kevin with her notebook in her coat, watches them go.
“Durkheim,” Margot says. “*Collective effervescence.* A society worshipping itself and calling it a football team.”
Laney turns her head exactly far enough to see the tailgate and no farther. “Then why are *you* crying?”
Margot wipes under one eye with the side of her thumb and inspects the thumb. “Allergies to the sacred.”

At the tailgate Kevin sits with one hand on the zipped pocket of his windbreaker, where Theo’s phone has lived since Kenner. Every so often Theo looks round at the pocket, and Kevin looks back at him, and Theo looks at the street.

body: Margot, on the tailgate, has been watching Kevin, and Kevin has been watching the band.
“You’re the only one not looking at them,” Margot says.
Kevin keeps his eyes on the sousaphone. “It’s a parade, Margot.”
Margot looks at him a little longer, and drops it.
By twenty to five the gray has begun to go to evening at the edges, and the band has stopped for water, and somebody on the neutral ground says, “Look what the river brought.”

He comes across the grass with two friends from Gentilly, one in a Deuce McAllister jersey and one in a purple Carnival wig worn for warmth: the Saints cap with the bent brim, a camouflage jacket, a go-cup in his hand. Wes is thinner than he was in October. It’s in his face mostly, under the cheekbones, and in how the jacket hangs off his shoulders. His eyes are bright, and a little slow.

Celeste gets to him first. “*Baby*,” she says, and takes his face in both her hands and looks at it, and lets go. Tony’s handshake gets about halfway before it turns into a hug with a fist in it, two thumps on the back. Tess turns Lucille round in her lap so he can see her, and Wes looks at the baby a long time, and puts out one finger and touches the foot of the snowsuit.
“Lucille,” Tess says.
Wes nods at the foot.

Lena works the buttons open from the inside, quick, and steps out of Jack’s coat into the wind and hugs Wes round the neck, up on her toes in the knit. He hugs her back with the go-cup held out away from her so it won’t spill on her.
“You eating, Wes?”
“Your mama’s gonna feed me, dawlin’.”
“Today, Wesley. I asked about today.”
He laughs at that, a little. She lets go of him and steps back, and back into Jack’s coat, and does the buttons up over herself, in front of him.
Wes watches her do it. The chipped tooth.
His eyes come to Jack, over the top of the knit. “Ohio.” He tips the go-cup at the two behind him. “Gentilly. They’re harmless.”
“Wes.”

A priest comes down the neutral ground in a black windbreaker with a gold Saints stole over it, a fleur-de-lis embroidered on each end, flinging holy water over the crowd off a palm branch he dips in a bucket that a boy carries along beside him. People duck and laugh and bless themselves. The Broussards cross themselves, Tony and Celeste and Remy, Tess with the baby’s mitten in her hand, Lena inside the coat with her elbow in Jack’s ribs, and Jack with them. Twenty feet up the curb Laney crosses herself too, backward, and then again the right way to be safe. Wes stands with the water on the brim of his cap and the go-cup in his hand.
When the priest has gone by, Wes turns to the street and tops the go-cup up from a flask out of his jacket, low, a quick pour. Inside the coat Lena is looking at it.

Then Lucille wants her bottle, suddenly and at the top of her lungs, and Celeste’s thermoses are the only hot thing on Canal Street. Tess gets up with the baby. Lena unbuttons herself out of Jack’s coat for the second time — “Hold my place” — and goes with them up the neutral ground to stand the bottle in a cup of hot coffee. Tony has already gone down the block with a cup for Luc, who won’t be allowed to drink it.

That leaves Wes and Jack at Tony’s empty chairs. Wes’s friends are a few yards off, arguing with a stranger about Deuce. Wes sits down in Tony’s chair and holds the go-cup on his knee and looks at the street. Jack stays standing, with his coat open and the wind back in it.

body.text: “How’s your brother?” Wes says.
“He’s got the Saints,” Jack says. “Him and one other guy in the dayroom.”
Wes laughs. It’s the old laugh, up out of the belly, and it’s gone nearly as soon as it comes.
“You never did answer me, podna,” Wes says. “On that beach. You raised that bottle, and I said that’s a yes where I’m from.”
He takes a pull on the go-cup and looks into it. “I been wondering was it a yes where *you’re* from.”
“You said you would, podna,” Wes says. “On that beach.” He takes a pull on the go-cup and looks into it. “I been wondering did you mean it.”
“You told me call her at eight-oh-four,” Wes says. He takes a pull on the go-cup and looks into it. “I did, a while. Then I didn’t.”
“You nodded, podna,” Wes says. “On that beach.” He takes a pull on the go-cup and looks into it. “I been thinking about that nod.”

journal.title: Wes Arceneaux
journal.text: Lena’s boyfriend. Tulane, civil engineering; the boat at sixteen. Six-two, a chipped front tooth, a Saints cap he’s been bending since 2006. Calls me the Ohio guy. Says she called me a jagoff and that means she likes me; he’s known her since she had a retainer. Drank the Pacific: the jar came back empty. Theo fetched him from the airport alone, in a two-seater, with a sign, and cancelled his motel. Bedbugs, Theo says. He’s on Theo’s new air mattress in our room, three nights. The Corps built the walls wrong; he’s going to build them right. I like him. Saturday night on the beach at Campus Point he waded into the Pacific to the knees. At sixteen he pulled people off roofs for four days in his uncle’s boat. There was one he couldn’t get to — a woman in an attic on Pauger Street; the axe wouldn’t go through. He couldn’t kneel for a year after. Then she came along, he says, and he could. Her Mémère gave him a ring at Easter, for when. He’s going to ask her father after she graduates. He asked me not to say anything to her. He asked me to take care of her. He stopped going to Mass in September. The attic wasn’t over. Mémère asked him about the ring at the tomb on All Saints. He ended it on All Souls, on the phone: she’d marry him anyway, he said, so he couldn’t let her. Tuesday at the parade, on the Canal Street neutral ground with two friends from Gentilly and a go-cup: thinner than in October, the same chipped tooth. Celeste called him baby. Lena hugged him. He asked about my brother, and about the beach. He hugged me goodbye this time.

s07a.slug: TUESDAY · 5:40 PM · CANAL STREET — A PRALINE
body: Lena comes back down the neutral ground at last, the bottle done and Lucille asleep at the truck, with the knit pushed up off her eyebrows, and steps into his coat again without looking, as if it were a doorway she uses, and he closes it. She’s cold all down the back from the walk to the truck, and it comes through the sweatshirt into him, and goes.

Josie is at his elbow. He didn’t hear her come. She has a praline in her mitten from the woman with the basket who has been working the curb since three, a dollar apiece, and she eats it in small bites with her eyes on the street.
“He gave Mémère the ring back,” Josie says. “In November. After Mass, in the box. She keeps it in the cedar chest in Breaux Bridge, with Grandmère’s christening gown.”
Lena, against his chest: “*Josie.*”
“He should know.”
“Know *what*, Josie.”
“*Rien.*” Josie breaks the praline in half, drops one half into the outside pocket of his coat at his hip, and goes on eating the other.

body.text: He has seen that ring once, on a screen the size of a matchbook that Wes had to tilt for him till it lit, on a lifeguard ramp at three in the morning, with the tide out below them.

body: Inside the coat Lena stays facing the street, her hands on his wrists where they cross over her.
Josie licks her mitten clean and goes back along the curb toward her mother.

body.text: Halfway there she turns and walks backward a few steps to say it, to Jack: “I didn’t tell Mémère. About Canada.”

body: Over Canal the gray is going to dark. The streetlights come on a block at a time, from up by the Dome down toward the river, one block and then the next, and the crowd cheers each block as it lights, because tonight this city will cheer anything that comes on. On the neutral ground the band stops to drink.

journal.title: Josie Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s sister, thirteen, with Lena’s eyebrows and Lena’s way of standing. Saturday night on the front steps she asked who I was talking to, and I told her. Sunday at breakfast she asked, at full volume, if my girlfriend in Canada was watching the game. When Mémère asked who was in Canada, she said *Personne*. Tuesday on Canal, with a praline: the ring went back to Mémère in November, after Mass, in its box. It’s in the cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. He should know, she said. Know what, Lena said. *Rien.*

s08.slug: TUESDAY · 6:50 PM · CANAL STREET — LOMBARDI GRAS
body: The noise gets there first. It comes down Canal a block ahead of anything you can see, the crowd up the street taking it up and handing it down, and by the time it reaches Tony’s corner the people around Jack are yelling at an empty street with their arms in the air.

Mounted police come first, at a walk, six abreast, the horses enormous under the streetlights with their ears going round at the noise. A marching band in purple and gold behind them, the drum line so loud it moves the air in his chest; another in green, the drum major bending over backward till his plume touches the street. And after the bands the floats, Carnival floats out of the krewe dens, papier-mâché and gold leaf and bulbs strung along their rails, borrowed for a Tuesday in February, and up on them in the cold, in jerseys and hoodies and fistfuls of black-and-gold beads, the players.

Drew Brees goes by on one of them, saluting the crowd, and every hand on the block goes to an eyebrow and salutes him back. Tom Benson rides another, and Tony takes his cap off to it. Remy, with somebody’s transistor against his ear, reports from the neutral ground that the floats are stopping up the route at a reviewing stand for the mayor. “Nagin’s up there somewhere,” Remy says.
Tony isn’t crying. He stands at the curb with his cap in his hand and his chin up and his face wet, and Celeste, beside him with her arm through his, says, “It’s the wind,” crying.
Pop would have stood here like that. Pop would have stood exactly here.

Laney has been catching beads with both hands since the first float, from twenty feet up the curb, and handing every strand to whatever child is nearest on a ladder. “Here, sugar.” A boy in a Bush jersey gets a purple one; a girl on her father’s shoulders gets three. A gold strand comes down out of the lights and she takes it one-handed, and comes down the curb through the crowd, and without a word or a look at Jack reaches over his shoulder and puts it in Lena’s hand. She is back up the curb before Lena has it doubled round her own wrist.
Margot stands with her hands deep in her coat pockets and her notebook in one of them. Theo keeps reaching into his good coat for a phone that isn’t there.

Behind the next band comes a float with a trophy on it as tall as a garage, a Lombardi built out of something silver and lit from underneath, and the crowd goes up at it like it’s the real thing, and surges, and the curb goes out from under everybody at once. Jack goes down a step into the gutter with Lena in the coat and gets his feet back. Her hand flies up to her collar. When the crowd settles back onto the curb she has her fist shut at her throat, and when she opens it the medal is in her palm with the chain run out between her fingers.
“Clasp,” she says.
She puts it in the breast pocket of her jean jacket, under his coat, and buttons the flap down over it.
At two minutes to seven, in the inside pocket of the Carhartt, against his ribs and against the middle of Lena’s back, the RAZR goes: one long buzz, the one it does for a picture.
She feels it. “You’re ringing.”
“It’s a text.”

He knows that buzz. There is one person on earth who sends him those. He doesn’t take it out. He couldn’t get to it without opening the coat, with her back where it is, and he leaves the coat shut, and it lies there against his ribs, between his shirt and her, and goes still. She doesn’t step out of the coat.

And then, up Canal, under the lights, the real one. Sean Payton is on a float with the Lombardi Trophy up over his head in both hands, bringing a hand down off it to blow kisses at the city, and the noise coming down the street in front of him is nothing Jack has a word for, not from Cleveland, not from anywhere.

response: He gets her up onto Clovis’s folding chair with his hands at her waist inside the coat, and the coat comes up with her, and so does half of him, one knee on the seat of the chair beside her boots, holding her steady while the trophy goes by under the lights. She sees it. She yells at it in Mémère’s French with both arms up out of his coat, and he keeps her up there through the whole float.

choices.text: “Graven image, Mr. Broussard. I’m only saying.”
response: “Graven image, Mr. Broussard,” Jack says, into the top of the knit. “I’m only saying.”
Tony, at the curb, doesn’t turn round. “*SON.*”
This time it’s a warning, and it gets heeded, and Lena laughs into his collar without a sound, her shoulders going against his chest.

choices.text: *Keep still and watch it go by.*
response: He keeps still. She keeps still. The trophy goes by over their heads with the streetlights in it, and she brings both hands up and puts them over his on the front of the coat, and keeps them there till it’s gone on down toward the river.

s09.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:10 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN TABLE — LUC
body: They walked home from Canal in the dark, all of them, through a city with nowhere to put everybody, and Luc nodded once more across the street from his barricade as they went. Now it’s past one and he can’t sleep. The phone has been in the front pocket of his jeans since Canal, and he can feel it against his hip through the sleeping bag, warm from him, a coal he hasn’t taken out.

He goes down the attic stairs in his socks, backward, the way they have to be gone down, a hand on each rail. At the foot of them Mémère is asleep on the daybed with her lamp off and her hands folded on her beads on top of the quilt, very small under it, her mouth a little open. He goes past her on the boards that don’t talk and down the hall of First Communions toward the one light left on in the house.

The kitchen light is on. Luc sits at the table in a white undershirt and the dark blue trousers of his uniform. His duty belt hangs off the back of the chair beside him with everything still on it, and his shirt hangs off the chair on the other side, the radio clipped to its shoulder and turned down to a murmur: a dispatcher a long way off, reading numbers to somebody else. In front of him is the plate his mother left in the oven under foil. The masking tape that said LUC on the Tupperware has gone across onto the foil, and the foil is folded back off red beans and rice, a piece of the pickled pork, the heel of the French bread. He eats fast and neat, the fork never resting. Aints III lies under his chair with his chin on Luc’s sock.
Luc looks up at him in the hall door, and at the gold still on his cheekbone.
“Sit.”

Jack sits. Luc reaches behind him without getting up and opens the refrigerator, and an Abita comes out of it and across the oilcloth, the cap knocked off against the table’s edge with the heel of his hand on the way. Jack takes it. He drinks a little and holds the rest.
“Sixteen hours,” Luc says. “Canal.”
“I saw you. You nodded.”

“I saw you.” Luc tears the bread. A piece of the pork goes down under the chair, and the dog takes it and puts his chin back on the sock. “We lost one tonight. Seventy-one years old. Went down when the trophy came by. His heart. On his feet, in his Saints jacket, with his daughter hanging on to his arm. Took EMS twenty minutes to get through to him. He was gone before they got there. Maybe before he got to the street.”
He eats.

“Natural causes,” Luc says. “That’s what it was. That’s all the report’s ever going to say, and it’s true. And his daughter’s going to tell it at Thanksgiving for forty years. *He died at the parade.*” He runs the bread round the rim of the plate. “That’s a good one. That’s one you don’t mind writing.”
The refrigerator hums. On the chair back, the dispatcher says a street name into the kitchen and lets go of the key. Jack works his thumbnail under the corner of the Abita’s label.
“Y’all go back to California next week,” Luc says.
“After Ash Wednesday.”
“Okay.” Luc nods at the plate, and the fork stops for the first time since Jack came in.

“First year I was on,” he says. “Spring of ’06. Gentilly. A man came back from Houston to gut his house. Everybody was gutting. He took it down to the studs by himself: the drywall, the carpet, the cabinets, the bed. Put it all out on the curb in a pile higher than his truck, and his wife stayed with her sister in Houston till he had it done. Gas came back on that block in March.” A forkful. “One night in April he sat down in what was left of his kitchen, and he didn’t turn the stove off.”
The label comes away under Jack’s thumbnail in a strip, soft from the cold, and he keeps going.

“There was a paper on the table,” Luc says. “Could’ve been a note. Could’ve been a list for Home Depot. The house was still wet; the paper was wet. My sergeant read it. I read it. You couldn’t have told anybody what it said.” He turns the fork over in his fingers and puts it down. “He wrote it *accidental*. So the wife could have the funeral Mass at St. Raphael’s with no whispering in the back pews. And so the policy would pay.”
The refrigerator shudders and goes quiet, and the kitchen is louder without it.
“Nobody lied,” Luc says. “He just didn’t write down what nobody could prove.”
He picks the fork back up and finishes the rice. Out in the front room the daybed creaks under Mémère and settles. Jack has the label off now. It lies on the oilcloth beside the bottle in a wet curl.
“You write some of them,” Luc says, to the last of the beans, “the way the family can live with.”

He wipes the plate clean with the heel of the bread and eats that too. When he looks up again it’s with the other look, the one from the cruiser window on Esplanade, and it goes to Jack’s face and stays on the left side of it, on the eyebrow, where the white line cuts through it and the hair never came back.
“Where’d you get that?”

journal.title: Luc Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s oldest brother; NOPD. Worked a barricade on Canal for the parade and nodded at us once across the street. At one in the morning he ate his mother’s plate at the kitchen table and told me two stories. You write some of them the way the family can live with. He doesn’t do that off the clock.

choices.key: At one in the morning at the Broussards’ kitchen table, Luc asked about your eyebrow. A fight, you said. A long time ago. You didn’t win. Nobody does, he said.
response: “A fight,” Jack says. “A long time ago.”
“You win?”
“No.”
Luc keeps the look on him a while, the same one, up from under his own eyebrows. “Nobody does.” He pushes his chair back. “I don’t do that off the clock.”

He rinses the plate at the sink and stands it in the rack. He puts the belt on standing up, by the back door, and it goes round him with everything on it, the leather creaking, and his hands do the buckle without him; then the shirt over the undershirt, the radio back on his shoulder, still talking. He has his hand on the back door before he says it.
“She’ll be down in a minute. She don’t sleep after a parade.”
The yard takes him. Jack sits with two-thirds of an Abita and a curl of wet label, and the dog under the empty chair.

choices.key: At one in the morning at the Broussards’ kitchen table, Luc asked about your eyebrow. You told him a nun did it, in third grade, with a ruler. Uh huh, he said.
response: “A nun,” Jack says. “Third grade. A ruler.”
“Uh huh.” Luc picks his teeth with a fingernail and gives that the length of time it deserves. “I don’t do that off the clock.”

He takes the plate to the sink, runs the water on it, and stands it in the rack. He gets into the shirt and the belt by the back door, and then his keys come out of the trouser pocket, a ring of them as big as a janitor’s, and he goes round it with his thumb in the light from the window till he has the one he wants. He holds it up like a thing he means to show Jack, and doesn’t.
“She’ll be down in a minute. She don’t sleep after a parade.”
Out front a truck door goes, and then an engine, going away up Dupre. The dog comes out from under the empty chair and lies down under Jack’s.

choices.key: At one in the morning at the Broussards’ kitchen table, Luc asked about your eyebrow. A jealous husband, you said, in Erie. He’s heard better at Central Lockup.
response: “A jealous husband,” Jack says. “Erie, Pennsylvania.”
“Erie.”
“Pennsylvania.”
“I’ve heard better at Central Lockup.” Luc doesn’t smile. Something at the corner of his mouth thinks about it and decides against. “I don’t do that off the clock.”

He rinses the plate and stands it in the rack, and dresses for the street by the back door, the belt, the shirt, the radio back on his shoulder. At the door his hand goes to the light switch beside the frame and stops there, and comes away, and he leaves the kitchen lit.
“She’ll be down in a minute. She don’t sleep after a parade.”
The back steps take his weight one at a time, and the yard has him, and the light stays on over the oilcloth for whoever it was left on for.

body: She comes down the hall in Remy’s sweatshirt and bare feet, and the linoleum must be cold, because she crosses it on the outside edges of them to the stove. Her hair is down and flattened on one side from the pillow. She takes the small pot off its nail, not the big one, and the milk out of the refrigerator, and warms it on the low blue ring, because that’s how Mémère does it, with a pinch of sugar from the bowl and her back to him, stirring with a teaspoon so it won’t catch.

body.text: The crawfish he painted on her cheekbone is half gone, scrubbed at and given up on; one curl of it is left, gold, by her ear. His own is still on him. He can feel it pull when he moves his face.
body.else: There’s gold in her hairline still, from the twins and the brush, a fleck at her temple she missed. His own fleur-de-lis is still on him. He can feel it pull when he moves his face.

body: She pours two cups. She puts one down in front of him on top of the wet curl of label without asking, and sits across the oilcloth with the other in both hands, and sets her LG down face-up by the sugar bowl. Laney’s gold strand is still doubled round her wrist from Canal, and it clicks against the cup. Her fingers go to her collarbone, to the place the medal lives, and find the neck of the sweatshirt, and come back to the cup.
“Was that Luc’s truck?”
“He ate.”

“He always eats.” She blows on the milk. “He texted Mama about the man at the trophy float. Mama texted me. On his feet, on Canal, with the trophy going by.” She crosses herself with the cup still in her hand, quickly, the way she does at a siren, and looks up at the ceiling. “Not a bad way to go, Lord, if You were asking. Which You weren’t.”
She drinks. He drinks. It’s too sweet and it’s exactly right.
“Wes looked thin,” she says.
“He came.”
Lena looks at him over the cup, and nods, slowly, like that was the right answer to something.

“And Remy,” she says, picking it up from wherever it was before she came downstairs, “swears that ladder on Canal is his by right because he carried it from the truck, when Daddy carried it from the truck, and Remy carried the *cooler*, the empty cooler, and then he stood on the top step for the length of the Brees float like it was him getting saluted. Pride goeth, Remy, I told him. Proverbs sixteen —”
On the oilcloth by the sugar bowl the LG lights up. The little screen on its outside says JULIAN.
She looks at it. She puts two fingers on the back of the phone and turns it over, face-down, without opening it, and the light goes out under it against the oilcloth.
“— and *then* the ladder goeth. And if he tries it again I’m knocking him off it myself.”

She drinks her milk. A minute goes, and the phone buzzes once more, face-down, rattling against the oilcloth toward the sugar bowl, and her hand comes down flat on it and keeps it still against the table until it stops. She leaves the hand where it is after that, and finishes the milk with the other one.

response: “Goodnight, Lena.”
She looks at him across the table, with the cup at her mouth, for long enough that he thinks she isn’t going to answer. “Night, Jack,” she says.
She takes the phone with her. He looks at the pot on the back of the stove, where the last of the milk has gone to skin.
“Your milk’s going to skin.”
“Let it.”

She stands up and drinks it off standing, skin and all, and makes a face at him over the bottom of the cup. She rinses the cup and stands it upside down in the rack beside Luc’s plate, and takes her phone with her.
He gets up and takes the small pot off the stove, and runs the water into it, and works the skin off the bottom with his thumb.
She lets him. Behind him a chair scrapes. “Night, Jack.”
When he turns from the sink with the pot dripping in his hand, the sugar bowl is where the phone was.

s10.slug: WEDNESDAY · 2:05 AM · THE ATTIC — SOMETHING FROM VANCOUVER
body: Back past the daybed at the foot of the stairs, where Mémère sleeps with her beads, and up the stairs a rung at a time with his hands, and his head up through the hatch into the cold. The box fan is off. Tonight the cold has come in under the roof instead, and the points of the nails over his mattress have each got a bead of it.

Kevin is asleep by the hatch on his back, zipped to the chin, with the rosary shut in his fist on his chest. Theo lies on the middle mattress with his hands folded and his face to the rafters, very still. Asleep, or doing a good impression of it; Jack can’t tell which, and doesn’t try.
He lies down under Remy’s Tiger and gets the RAZR out of his jeans at last, and opens it under the sleeping bag on its cracked hinge, and the screen lights his hands green.

*SKYE (MISFIT) · New Picture Msg · 6:58 PM.* The little envelope with the paperclip on it, unopened. Under it, the texts that came in on the same burst, the ones the phone could carry without asking him anything.

body: In the duffel by his head the swing print is still in Hale’s *Moviegoer*, face-down, NOT FOR POSTING across the back of it in her Sharpie.

*The darkroom.* The red bulb and the timer going, the prints of him drying on their line, and *No.*, the first one she ever said to him and meant. He has carried that the length of Interstate 10 in a van with five other people in it, and up these stairs tonight, and it is still exactly as close as it was.

The streetlight comes in through the gable window past the dead fan and lies across the foot of his mattress. Kevin breathes, and turns over once in his sleeping bag with a sound like a grocery sack, and is still. The cold beads on the nails. He holds the phone under the sleeping bag with his thumb over the key.

choices.key: At two in the morning in the Broussards’ attic you opened what Skye sent from Vancouver. It was yours.
response: He opens it.

The RAZR goes to work on it, and it comes down the little screen from the top a band at a time, postage-stamp small, gray and then less gray, and he brings the phone out from under the sleeping bag and tilts it up to the streetlight until the grain settles. The first band is plaid. He knows it before anything else in it, the elbow worn thin: his shirt, which wardrobe must have given up for a night, spread out flat under her on a hotel bed, the collar turned up by her cheek. Then her face, upside down to him until he turns the phone, because she took it from above, blind, the 3GS held out over herself at the end of her arm, so the frame runs crooked down the length of the bed toward a gray window and her own forearm cuts across one corner of it, huge and out of focus. Her head is pushed back off the pillow. Her eyes are shut and her mouth is open. Every one she has ever sent him knew exactly where his eyes would be — dared them, asked them, laughed at them — and this one isn’t looking for anybody at all. Down the length of her, bare in that window light, her other hand is between her thighs, and it is the one thing in the picture the camera couldn’t keep: it has gone to a blur. She didn’t stop to aim. She didn’t stop.

He lies under the beaded nails with the phone close to his face, and somewhere in the second band he stopped breathing. His body answered before he did: he is hard against the zipper of his jeans, and his free hand has shut on a fistful of nylon. Four feet off, Kevin sleeps with a rosary shut in his fist. A floor below, an old woman sleeps on her beads. Half a continent away is that bed, and every part of him wants to be in it.
He answers with one thumb, slowly, the keys going in one letter at a time, because it’s T9, and because the hand isn’t steady.

s11.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:50 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT ROOM — SAINTE SCHOLASTIQUE
body: Wednesday comes up clear. The gable window goes from gray to the thin pale gold of a cold morning, and the box fan stands in it with its blades still, and past the fan the roofs of Mid-City are wet and pitched every which way and steaming a little where the sun gets to them first.

Jack says the penance at the window, on his knees on the boards in his socks, with his breath fogging the glass. The sixth morning. His voice has come back up out of the gravel far enough to use, and he keeps it low for the attic. *He summoned the Twelve and began to send them out two by two.* It goes the way it went yesterday, every word where he left it, down to the oil. *And they anointed with oil many who were sick —*
He stops there, and says it again. *They anointed with oil many who were sick.* Then the rest, *and cured them*, and he crosses himself and stays on his knees, looking out.

Down on Dupre Street the city is going back to work. A man in hospital scrubs scrapes the dew off his windshield with a CD case. Somebody’s car radio comes on in the middle of a traffic report, the first Jack has heard since Friday, and a woman on WWL says the Pontchartrain Expressway is moving normally, as if that were news, and this morning it is.
Behind him Kevin is sitting up on his sleeping bag by the hatch with his shoes already tied. “Laney says nine o’clock,” he says. “She has a list. It has sections.”
From the middle mattress, out of the pillow, Theo: “Tell her I’ve gone ahead in spirit.”

The front room has its lamp on. Mémère is in her armchair with her chicory, dressed and pinned, the daybed behind her already made, and the house is coming past her in its work clothes. Celeste comes through from the kitchen in navy scrubs with her Touro badge clipped to the pocket and her car keys out, and kisses the top of her mother’s head on the way by, and stops in the door.
“Back by six, baby,” she says, to the front room in general. Her eyes are on Jack when she says it.

The twins go out ahead of her to the bus in their uniform polos with their Saints hoodies over them, Josie objecting to Wednesday as a concept, Jude carrying both their lunches. Remy comes down the hall with his duffel on his shoulder and a go-cup of his mother’s coffee and bends for Mémère’s kiss.
“I got a test,” he tells her. “Allegedly. I’ll be back Friday for Endymion.”
“*Étudie.*”
“That’s what I said, Mémère.” And the screen door, and the Suburban turning over at the curb.

When the door has stopped swinging Mémère holds out her hand, and Josie, back in at a run for her permission slip, unhooks the parish calendar from its nail by the kitchen phone and brings it to her. St. Jude has been holding up January for ten days past his time. Mémère lifts him by the corner, up and over, and smooths February down on her knee: Our Lady in a grotto, and a girl in a white headscarf kneeling in front of it with her hands together. She puts her finger on the tenth.
“*Sainte Scholastique*,” she says, and Josie takes the calendar back to its nail and is gone again.

body.text: Over the rim of the cup Mémère’s eyes come up to Jack, in the doorway with his boots in one hand. “You receive in the hand,” she says. “Left over the right, like a throne. Somebody taught you.”

“*Bon.*” She drinks her chicory. “Lucien noticed.”

body: Lena is in the hall door in jeans and a Broussard’s Seafood sweatshirt older than the twins, with her hair up wet and her father’s second ring of keys hooked on one finger and a cup in her other hand. Her collar is open, and there is nothing at her throat. She holds the cup out to him.
“It’s half,” she says. “You came down late.”
He takes it. It’s made her way, with too much sugar in it, and he drinks it anyway, standing in her grandmother’s front room in his socks.

Tony fills the front door in his market jacket with his own keys out. “God was willing,” Tony announces, in case anybody in the house had doubts about the sign. He looks at Jack. “Ohio. You know ice?”
“I’m on the register,” Lena says, to Jack, not to her father. “Reopening days I’m always on the register. I’ve been on it since I could reach the drawer.”

At the foot of the attic stairs Laney stands in a robe and full makeup with a sheet of Broussard’s notepaper written on both sides. “Café du Monde,” she reads. “The Cathedral. The river. Beignets, twice, on purpose.” She looks at the keys on Lena’s finger, and at the cup in Jack’s hand, and reaches out and knocks twice on the banister. “Nine o’clock. Y’all come or y’all don’t come. I am not *telling* anybody *anything*.”
On the stairs behind her Margot is already in her coat, and Kevin is behind Margot. In the front door Tony waits, and jingles.

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners. The Friday before I flew back she took the phone for ten seconds to ask was I eating. When I come to New Orleans I come to her house first. Thursday at seven in the morning she called me herself, from Dupre Street, on a number the redhead gave her. She knew I’d said yes. She called anyway: I don’t come because the rich boy asked me, I come because she asked me. Don’t bring nothing. Come to this house first — I said it back to her. Lena told her not to call. Saturday night on the porch she cancelled Theo’s hotel. You sleep here. Boys in the attic. She sleeps in the front room, where she can see the stairs. Sunday she was dressed for the eight o’clock before seven, in her chair with the lamp on. Two of you are up; the other sleeps like a Protestant. For the game she put Lena and me on the floor, in front, where she could see us. Wednesday at dawn she turned the parish calendar to February: *Sainte Scholastique*. She watched how I received on Sunday. Left over the right. Somebody taught you.

s11m.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:40 AM · BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD, BANKS STREET
body: Broussard’s Seafood smells like the Gulf in the cold: ice, and brine, and last week’s crab boil still down in the floor drains under this morning’s bleach, and coffee from a Mr. Coffee on top of the ice machine that Tony set going the minute he had the door unlocked. It’s one long room under a pressed-tin ceiling painted white too many times: the glass case down the left side, an oyster bench under the front window, the walk-in at the back behind a steel door with a handle like a slot machine’s, and in the middle of the concrete floor a drain that the whole room has been pitched toward since before Lena was born.

The first thing Tony does is go to the door. The sign is still taped inside the glass in his marker — CLOSED · WHO DAT · BACK WEDNESDAY · GOD WILLING — and he works the tape off the corners with his thumbnail, careful of the paper, and folds it in four and puts it in his shirt pocket and buttons the flap down over it. He turns the card on the door to OPEN. He doesn’t say what he wants the sign for.

Lena throws Jack a pair of white rubber boots from the back with no warning at all, one and then the other. “Daddy’s spares. Two pair of socks.” While he’s on one foot getting the second boot on, she comes up behind him with a rubber apron and drops it over his head, takes the strings out of his hands, and ties them at the small of his back, quick, a double knot pulled tight. Her knuckles are against his spine through the flannel for as long as a knot takes. He stands at the open case with the cold coming up off it into his face and doesn’t turn around, and when he does she is at the register with the drawer out, counting the bank.

Then the ice. It comes out of the machine in flakes, and he shovels it into the case by the scoop and banks it high at the back and runs it down toward the glass, so the melt has somewhere to go and the somewhere is the drain. Nothing sits in its own water. That is Gloria’s first rule of the Anchor’s walk-in, given to him in September over a tub of shrimp somebody else had let drown, and it turns out to be a law of the Gulf. In Youngstown the word *bank* was for furnaces, a fire covered over at night so it would still be alive in the morning. Gloria uses it for ice. He has stopped hearing the difference.

The shrimp go in steel pans nested down in the ice, heads all one way, toward the glass, so they look like they’re coming to you. The fish go on top of the bed, never under it: two red snapper, a black drum, a sheepshead with its strange square human teeth, laid out with their eyes clear. Gloves on for the ice, off for the lemons. Tony is at the scale at the end of the case sorting the first pan, and for ten minutes he watches Jack do it and says nothing. Jack can feel him not saying it. He finishes the front lip with the back of the shovel, and the meltwater finds its way across the floor to the drain, and goes.
“Who taught you ice?”
“A woman named Gloria.”
Tony thinks about it. “Bring her.”

Mr. Alcide comes in at eight, in a Saints toboggan and a rubber apron of his own, and takes the stool at the oyster bench under the window. He’s small and seventy-something, with forearms like the rope on a crab trap, and his radio lives on the shelf over the bench, a red plastic Panasonic held together with electrical tape. Boozoo Chavis is on it, and he sings along under it in a French that isn’t the record’s. He opens oysters slower than Jack expected, and every one comes open clean: the knife in at the hinge, a turn of the wrist, the top shell into the bucket, the oyster cut loose and turned over in its own liquor without a nick on it.
“Forty-one years,” Tony says at the scale, watching him. “You can tell a man by how he holds a knife.”

Between oysters Mr. Alcide gives the room his opinion of the Indianapolis Colts, in French, at length. At one point he puts the knife down to show how the pass to Tracy Porter was thrown: from the hip, underhand, an old woman scattering corn for the chickens.
“He says the Colts were worthy opponents,” Lena says from the register.
“That didn’t sound worthy.”
“It’s what he meant. In his heart.”

At ten past eight Tony’s flip phone goes off on the scale, and he puts it on speaker without wiping his hands. A big man’s voice comes out of it, with an outboard idling behind it and gulls, and Breaux Bridge in every vowel.
“Antoine. You sober?”
“I’m *open*.”
“*Bon.* Then the boy’s on his way, and I’m going to bed.”
“Nonc Placide,” Lena tells Jack. “Daddy’s big brother. He shrimps all night out of Empire and calls in the morning to see is Daddy drunk.”

Twenty minutes later a kid in white boots backs a pickup to the door with two ice chests in the bed, and Jack takes one end of each and Tony the other. On the lid of the first somebody has painted MISS ODILE by hand in blue house paint.
“His boat,” Lena says. “Named for Mémère.”

By nine the regulars are coming, one man in a Saints bathrobe over his work clothes, all of them with the gray faces of a city that has been up since Sunday, and they tell Tony about the parade, and Tony tells it back to each of them, a little bigger every time.

And Lena. Jack has watched her take rooms apart at Marisol since August. He has never seen her on her own ground. Home field. She rings a man up and has his change counted back into his palm before the drawer has finished coming out, and bumps the drawer shut with her hip. An old man in a feed cap comes in for his dozen, and she gets him with both her hands around his one, in Mémère’s French first, *Mon beau*, Mr. Theriot, and then in English, for the room: “I gave up on you. I was about to give your oysters to a younger man.” When he asks her which younger man, she tips her head down the case at Jack, who is in a rubber apron holding a red snapper by the gill. “That one. He’s from Ohio. He wouldn’t know what he had.” Mr. Theriot studies Jack, and the snapper, and takes his oysters.

Then the crab man calls. She takes the wall phone the length of the case on its long cord, looks down into the bushel baskets on the floor, where the morning’s crabs are alive and furious, and pushes her sleeves up to the elbow.

“Mr. Dupuy. Mr. Dupuy. Did you look in these baskets before you put them on the truck, or did you send your nephew to look, because your nephew can’t tell a number one from a cinder block. No, sir. No, *sir*. They are not ones. Half of them are sooks. Sweet suffering Saint Sebastian, Mr. Dupuy, they’ve got their *fingernails painted*. I’m standing over a basket of girls dressed for Endymion and you are charging me for heavy males.” Down at the bench Mr. Alcide has put his knife down to listen. “No, sir. Here’s what you’re going to do. I’ll pay you twos for the sooks and ones for the ones, and you are going to thank me, because Daddy would have sent the whole truck back to Lafitte with a note on it.” A pause, while Mr. Dupuy, wherever he is, works out that he is going to thank her. “Thank you, Mr. Dupuy. Kiss Miss Rita for me.”
She puts the receiver back on its hook. Mr. Alcide picks up his knife and says the only English he has said all morning. “*That* one.”

In the lull after it a woman in a plastic rain bonnet with a Saints scarf tied over it, who announces to the room that she has known Lena since the car seat sat on top of that very register, looks down the case at Jack, who is banking ice into the hole the morning has made in it.
“This your fella, Lena?”
Lena counts the woman’s change out into her hand. “This is Jack, Miss Earline. He knows ice.”
The woman accepts this. “Ice is a start,” she says, and takes her shrimp.
Jack puts another scoop of ice where it goes.

It’s getting on for ten when Tony comes down the case with a fresh pan of Placide’s shrimp to put out. Lena is on the phone again at the far end with the cord stretched out to the walk-in, and Mr. Alcide’s radio is going, and Tony sets the pan down in the ice Jack banked and moves the big ones to the front with his hand, with his eyes on the shrimp.

body.text: “You put the good ones in front, son,” he says. “A man can’t keep two cases full.” And he goes back to the scale.
body.else: “Reopened in ’06 on a generator and a prayer,” he says. “We sold to the people who came back. Then we sold to the people who came back after them.” And he goes back to the scale.

journal.title: Tony Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s father. Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Twenty-eight years in the same seats. Held the phone up to the kitchen radio for the whole second half while we lost him at every curve on Highway 1. Wes told him there’s a Browns fan out here. Laney had him at hello. Saturday night in the side yard he put me on the paddle inside ten minutes. Sunday in the pew he told God He owes him one. He wouldn’t watch the game; he listened on the porch, on the radio, with his eyes shut. When it was over he cried face-down on the hood of a stranger’s car, and then he picked me up off the street. Wednesday the market opened again and he put me behind the case. Who taught you ice, he said. A woman named Gloria. Bring her.

Tony nods at the scale, and puts a pound of shrimp on it, and the needle swings and settles. He bags them, and twists the bag, and writes the price on it with the grease pencil from behind his ear.
Over the door the bell goes, and lets in Banks Street and a man in a Saints poncho who wants three pounds of the big ones, the ones in front.

Tony’s hand stops on the shrimp. He looks at Jack over the pan for a while, a big man in a rubber apron with his face gone quiet, and then he nods, once, and sets the big ones a little straighter.

Over the door the bell goes, and two nurses coming off the night shift at Touro come in off Banks Street in their scrubs and their Saints toboggans, wanting a pound of the big ones and the parade, and Tony gives them both.
