Tony laughs. It starts down in the big body and comes up all at once, and he has to put a hand on the scale.

Over the door the bell goes, and two nurses coming off the night shift at Touro come in off Banks Street in their scrubs and their Saints toboggans, wanting a pound of the big ones and to hear about the parade, and Tony, still wiping his eyes, tells them.

body: The sun is out over Jackson Square after Tuesday’s gray, thin and low and cold, and the Square has come out to meet it. Painters are hanging canvases on the iron fence. A woman at a card table sets down a deck of tarot cards and a thermos and pours the first cup of her shift. Mules in blankets stand in a row along Decatur with their carriages behind them and their breath going up, and in the middle of it all General Jackson sits his rearing bronze horse with his hat raised and a pigeon on it.

Café du Monde is packed to the curb under its green-and-white awning. It took two buses and a walk, forty-one minutes by Kevin’s watch. Laney takes the one table with five chairs and orders for it before anybody is sitting, in a Dallas soprano that reaches the kitchen.

“Three orders of beignets, sir, that’s nine, I counted. Three café au laits. One hot chocolate for the fireman, because he is a child. And a black coffee for the Scandinavian, who is dead inside and proud of it.”
“Accurate,” Margot says.
“Yes, baby,” says the waiter, who writes none of it down, and goes.
Laney sits very straight. “He called me *baby*.”
“He called Kevin baby at the door,” Margot says.
“He meant it, too,” says Kevin.
She has the Broussard’s Seafood notepaper unfolded beside her saucer, and Jack, reading it upside down, sees that the day has been divided into sections.

body.title: Laney’s list (Broussard’s Seafood notepaper, front)
body.text:
I. SUSTENANCE — Café du Monde (beignets x2, put down on purpose)
II. DEVOTION — the Cathedral (Kevin)
III. EDUCATION — that museum (Margot, do NOT let her start)
IV. THE RIVER (Theo, same)

body: The beignets come three to a plate under a drift of powdered sugar deep enough to lose a fork in. Jack’s hot chocolate is thick enough to stand a spoon in. Margot wraps one beignet in a napkin and puts it in her coat without explanation, and Kevin, who has given the warning at the bus stop, on the transfer and at the curb on Decatur, gives it a fourth time. “Do not exhale over the plate.”
Theo, in the camel coat, takes a pastry in both hands. “Picture it,” he says, and draws the breath for it. “A man, a coat, a pastry —”
He lets the breath go. The sugar rises in a single soft detonation past his face, hangs in the sun, and settles on him from collar to hem.
“Bless his heart,” Laney says. “He never could hold it in.”
“I said it four times,” says Kevin. “That’s a mass-casualty event.”
Theo holds both arms out from his sides and lets the last of it settle. “I’ve been *floured*,” he says.
“You look like a Buick on Glenwood Avenue after the first snow,” Jack says.

“People love a Buick.” Theo accepts the loss of rank, and eats, and when the plate is clean he wraps the last beignet in a napkin and puts it in the pocket of the coat, where it can do no further harm.

The Cathedral stands across the Square behind its palms and its black iron, three spires and a clock face, and Kevin is already up and crossing to it at a walk that is just short of a run. At the foot of the steps he takes off his windbreaker and folds it over his arm, as he does at any church door in any weather.

Theo has dropped onto the nearest bench with the sugar still coming off his shoulders. “I’ll hold the coats,” he says. Laney sits down beside him and hooks her arm through his. Kevin hands over the windbreaker, and Theo lays it across his knees with the zipped pocket up, the confiscated phone a small flat lump in it.
“Costigan. Coat.”
“I’m good.” The RAZR and Lena’s tin ride in the Carhartt’s inside pocket, and it stays on.

Inside it is colder than the Square, a cold that comes up through his boots, and the sun comes in red and blue off the high windows and doesn’t warm a pew. On an easel inside the door a card gives the day in careful capitals: *Wednesday. Memorial of St. Scholastica, virgin.* Mémère’s finger on the calendar at seven this morning, and here the saint is again.

Kevin goes straight to the rack of votive candles at the side altar, puts a dollar through the slot of the box, lights a candle from another candle, and lights a second from the first. He says nothing about either. He walks up to a pew near the front and kneels with his forehead on his folded hands, and is still.

Jack takes a pew three rows back and kneels too. He says the Hail Mary because it is what he has. At the rack a boy about Rosie’s size is up on his toes with a taper nearly as long as he is, and his mother’s hands hover under his elbows the whole time he reaches.
Margot is waiting at the foot of the steps when they come out into the glare, with a paper napkin in her hand. She holds it out to Kevin without looking at him.
“Control group,” she says. “I set it aside at the table. I wanted to know if they hold.”
Kevin unwraps the beignet and bites it. “Do they?”
“They hold.” Margot turns to Jack. “Did you pray, or observe?”
“Hail Mary. Mostly I watched a kid light a candle.”

“A recognized methodology.” She has already turned to the building next along, where a sign by the museum door has been waiting for her all morning. “The room where a continent changed hands,” she reads, off the building and the sign at once.

Kevin goes across to the bench for his windbreaker. Theo hands it up without a word, and Kevin runs a thumb down the zip of the inside pocket and puts it on. From where she sits, forty feet off, Laney’s voice crosses the walk with no effort at all. “On a *Wednesday*?”
Margot reads the sign again from the top, as if it might have changed, and does not answer.

From a shop door up Chartres a soprano saxophone is working through something slow and French over the scratch of a very old record. Jack stops in the sun to hear it out, a minute and a half of tune and the needle at the end, and then goes after the others across Decatur and up the long steps to the Moonwalk.

At the top the river is just there, all at once, wider than anything has a right to be: brown, and moving, and cold from the far bank to the toes of his boots. A towboat shoves a raft of barges upstream against the current, a Lordstown parking lot of red steel making about the speed of a man walking. Across the water Algiers is a low line of warehouses with the sun full on them.
Theo and Laney are along the rail with their backs to him and their heads together, Laney’s hands going the way they go when she is explaining something for the second time.
“— we don’t *touch* it, we don’t *say* it, we don’t even look *straight* at it —”
“At what?” Jack says.
Laney doesn’t turn. “My birthday,” she says, without a breath, and then she turns, full around, with a smile the width of the Mississippi. “It’s Sunday. Y’all are not to do *anything*.”
“She means it,” Theo says, half a second behind. “Last year somebody hired a mariachi.”
“*Mama* hired a mariachi.”
“Nine men. One of them was a cousin.”
“Eight.”
“Eight,” Theo says. “One of them was a cousin.”
“I’ll tell the mariachi,” Jack says.
“Tell him gently.”

Kevin and Margot come up the steps behind Jack, Kevin with the last of the beignet and Margot with her hands in her coat. Laney rounds on them. “It is decided. We plan *nothing* for Sunday, because planning is how you jinx it.”
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, “that’s the first good plan either of you has had.”
Margot looks from Laney to Theo to the river. “I’m amending a note from Monday,” she says.
“Margot, honey, *no*.” Laney hooks an elbow through Kevin’s and another through Margot’s and steers them off along the boardwalk toward a ship that has suddenly become urgent. Kevin looks back once.
That leaves Theo at the rail. The wind takes a streak of sugar off his shoulder and carries it out over the water, and he watches it go.
“Whatever this week is, Costigan —” He stops, and looks at the river.
“Never mind,” he says. “It’s a good week.”

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas. Thursday night he’d already paid my share. I made him take it back. He took a call from his mother at the edge of the lot: sandbags; they’re saying rain Friday night on the hill. At a quarter to five he hugged Skye a long time and said something only she heard. Friday night at a gas station in El Paso, by the ice machine, he and Laney said it was a mistake. The whole thing. I agreed with them. He went in and paid for the gas himself. Wednesday at Café du Monde he lost his whole camel coat to powdered sugar. He stayed outside the Cathedral and held the coats. On the Moonwalk he started to tell me something about the week, and thought better of it.

choices.key: On the Moonwalk Theo started to say something about this week, and stopped, and said it’s a good week. It is, you said.
response: “It is,” Jack says.

Theo nods at the river. Twice, short, and his mouth goes with it as though he is agreeing to terms. A towboat far downstream puts out one long note, and the wind takes the note and another streak of sugar off his shoulder together and carries both toward the Gulf.
“Say it again on Sunday,” Theo says.
“It’s a birthday. Nothing’s happening.”
“Say it anyway.”
From the top of the steps Laney’s voice comes down the levee in full soprano. “*Theodore! Jack!* Margot has found a fortune-teller with a Ph.D., and they have started in on *methodology*!”

choices.text: “You’ve got sugar on your conscience, Vance.”
choices.key: On the Moonwalk Theo said it’s a good week. You told him he’s got sugar on his conscience. His conscience is cashmere, he said. It brushes off.
response: Theo looks down at his lapel, where the powder lies in the fold of the camel, and then at Jack.

“My conscience is cashmere,” he says. “It brushes off.” He brushes it, one slow stroke across his chest with the side of his hand, and a white streak goes out over the rail and down toward the water. “See?” Some of it doesn’t come off, and he leaves it. “Yours is wool, Costigan. Itches like sin and never wears out.”
Jack looks down at the Carhartt — canvas, a tin and a phone in the pocket, Interstate 10 in the seams — and has no argument.

choices.key: On the Moonwalk Theo started to say something about this week. You asked him what. Nothing, he said. Eat your beignet.
response: “Theo. What?”

“Nothing.” Theo laughs, short, before the question is all the way out, and digs in the pocket of the camel coat and comes up with the napkin. The beignet has taken the shape of the pocket. “Eat your beignet.”

Jack takes it. It is cold and flat and still very good, and the sugar goes down the front of the Carhartt where Theo’s went down the camel. Theo watches the barges push upstream, one raft and then another behind it, slower than anything that gets anywhere. He offers nothing else, and Jack finishes the beignet.

s12.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:10 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT STEPS — THE MOON

body.text: He comes home from Banks Street a little after three with the Gulf in his clothes. Tony kept him on to hose the floor down to the drain and stack the empty ice chests, MISS ODILE on top, and his hands are red to the wrists from the ice. Lena walked home ahead of him at two with her father’s second ring of keys, and with the carnations she bought out of the florist’s bucket by the door next to the market, at lunch, out of her own apron pocket.
body.else: He comes home from the Quarter a little after three on the bus up Esplanade, with powdered sugar worked into the front of the Carhartt that no amount of slapping at it on the bus has moved. He left Theo and Laney and the others at the river with a list that had sections. Lena got home from the register before him.

body: She’s on the porch swing in the Broussard’s Seafood sweatshirt with her boots up on the rail and her father’s keys in her fist, and her hair coming down out of its pencil. Beside her on the slats lies a small bunch of white carnations wrapped in the classifieds out of Monday’s paper. She watches him come up the walk.

The afternoon is clear and hard and blue, the cold that came in behind the parade still sitting on the city. Dupre Street has gone back to work: a mail truck working its way down the block from the corner, two doors down a man up a ladder taking a Saints flag down off his gutter and folding it over his knee. At the curb the Odyssey sits under its dust with WHO DAT · 1 DAYS still on the back glass and Josie’s lipstick zero gone pink and smeary in three days of weather.

He sits down on the top step, and the RAZR goes against his ribs. The little window on the lid says SKYE (MISFIT). Behind him the swing stops. When he opens the phone and turns his head to get it to his ear, Lena is watching him do it. He gets up and takes it down the walk to the gate, the way he’d take any call off anybody’s porch, and leans on the post.
“This is Burnaby,” Skye says. “Burnaby would like to know where you are.”
“At the front gate.”
“Whose front gate.”
“The man on the porch’s. In Mid-City.”
“Oh good. Stay there. I can picture that.” A generator hums under her, and somebody close by yells for a C-stand, and doesn’t get it, and yells again.

body.text: She doesn’t ask. She lets the man yell for his C-stand a third time and waits on the other end of it.
“I got it,” Jack says, low, to the street. “Last night. I was by myself.” Up the block the mail truck stops and starts. “It was yours. I could tell.”
On her end a door shuts, and the lot is gone, and there’s only the generator through a wall.
“I’ve never sent anybody one I didn’t take *for* them,” Skye says.
Right behind it she laughs at herself, short, through her nose. “That’s a terrible thing to say on a lunch break. Forget I said it on a lunch break. Remember it some other time.”
“Did you get it?”
He tells her the truth, low, because it’s her asking. “I got it. I opened it. Then I erased it.”
On her end a door shuts, and the lot is gone, and there’s only the generator through a wall. The mail truck stops two houses up and the carrier gets out with a bundle.
“Okay,” Skye says. “That one was yours to erase.”

“So,” Skye says. “I read your midnight text. You deleted my best work unopened, in a Catholic grandmother’s house. That’s the most respectful thing anyone’s ever done to me, and I want to file a complaint.”
“Take it up with the grandmother.”

“I bet she has a *form*. I bet it’s in French.” The C-stand man gives up. When she speaks again she has moved off somewhere, or put her back to a wall, and her voice is down close to the phone. “Was it the house, or was it you?”
Jack looks at the Odyssey at the curb, the lipstick zero.
“Both,” he says.
A gust comes up Dupre Street and turns the newspaper over on the carnations. In Burnaby a door shuts on the lot. “…Okay,” Skye says. “Both I can work with.”

body: “News from the North,” she says, back at full speed. “The torch came through today.”
“The Olympic one?”

body.text: “Is there a lesser torch? A man in a white tracksuit ran past craft services with fire, and everybody clapped like it was a person. Russ cried. Kyle tried to get a picture of it and got the back of a Mountie.” A plastic lid comes off something. “And we reshot Wade. The porch. The light was wrong on Monday, apparently, the light was *lying*, so we did it all again, and the beard did your pause, and I cried again.” The lid goes back on. “They came. That’s the worst part. They come when they’re called now.”

body: “That’s the job.”

“That’s the job,” she says, “and I hate how much I like it.” Somebody knocks on her door and says *Cassie, hair*, all run together. “Hair,” Skye says. “They want to make it worse. Quick, before they do. Did the man on the porch open up?”
“Seven this morning. God was willing. It was on the sign.”
“What happened to the sign?”

body.text: “He folded it in four and buttoned it in his shirt pocket.”
body.else: “I don’t know. I was in the Quarter, eating sugar.”

body.text: “Of course he did. That’s a man who keeps a sign. I knew that about him from Canada.”
body.else: “Find out. I need to know what happens to the sign. I’m invested in the sign.”

body.text: “Okay. I have to go be Cassie, and I’m on until they run out of dark. Remember the moon.”
body.else: “Okay. I have to go be Cassie, and I’m on until they run out of dark. New rule. If I text you the moon, it means I’m working all night and you’re not allowed to worry.”

body: When he looks back up at the porch, the swing hasn’t moved. Lena has her boots crossed on the rail and the keys gone still in her hand, and she is looking at the van at the curb.
“Tonight’s the moon,” Skye says.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked. She was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. She drove me up the hill at three and waited in the Saab under the bell tower with three suitcases in the back. Friday at a quarter to five she stood with us in the lot while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south. Friday at a truck stop under Picacho Peak she called from Burnaby. Wardrobe took my flannel: Cassie wears it; it got the part. The geese are the size of Labradors. I read her one of Hale’s rude ones at the pump. Saturday night she called again after wrap, and I read her two more, on the Broussards’ front steps. I told Lena’s little sister who she is. My girlfriend. In Canada. She wants a call at the kickoff. Sunday at the kickoff I had the phone open to call her, and it rang in my hand. She was in a trailer in Burnaby in a Colts cap, wearing it into Cassie’s wig. She bought her own *Moviegoer* at the airport and read it on the plane. Being in the movie doesn’t make anything real either, she says. She owes me a picture. She turned her TV off to hear the kickoff on Dupre Street. Her text after the game got to me at a quarter to four in the morning, on Esplanade. She’s taking full credit. Monday she called at her lunch from Burnaby: she cried for real in the Wade scene and the director kept it. Wednesday the torch went past craft services, and she’s shooting all night. That’s what the moon means.

s12a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:20 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH — UP THERE
body: The mail truck comes level with the house, and the carrier, a heavy man in a Saints toboggan with the USPS jacket over it, hands the Broussards’ mail to Jack over the gate and says “Who dat” for good afternoon. Jack says it back. The truck goes on down Dupre Street toward the bayou, and he carries the mail up the walk.
From the swing Lena says, “Is she all right? Up there?”
He stops on the bottom step with the mail. She has the keys in her lap and her eyes on him, and the carnations in their newspaper beside her.
“She’s working all night.”
Lena takes her boots down off the rail, one and then the other, and the swing goes back under her and comes forward and she lets it. “Then she’s all right.”

She stands up off the swing with the keys in one hand and the carnations in the other and comes down the steep steps to him. Up close the carnations smell faintly of cloves, and of wet stems and newsprint, and somebody has written the price on the paper in ballpoint, a dollar fifty. She takes the mail off him and drops it on the swing, and puts the carnations in his hands, stems first.
“Come on,” she says, and goes past him down the walk.

s13.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:45 PM · ST. LOUIS CEMETERY NO. 3, ESPLANADE AVENUE — THE GUIDRY TOMB
body: The sun has started down, low enough already to get in under the oaks, and it lies along the Esplanade neutral ground in long bars, yellow and no warmer for it. They walk up the avenue toward the bayou on the side with the old houses, Lena with her hands in the pockets of her jean jacket and the strand from Laney still doubled round her wrist, Jack carrying the carnations like he was sent to the store for them. They pass Holy Rosary. Father Hébert’s car is in the lot behind the church with a black-and-gold flag on its antenna. She doesn’t slow down.

The cemetery is the next block, almost at the water: a long white wall along the avenue and an iron gate standing open in it, and inside the gate a man in a cap on a folding chair with a ring of keys on his knee and a radio going low, who looks at the carnations and nods them in.

Inside it’s a town. The tombs stand shoulder to shoulder down narrow lanes with names on the corners, little white houses for the dead with peaked roofs and iron fences, some no bigger than a toolshed and some like chapels. Plaster saints with their noses gone. A few have split along a seam and been patched with brick. In Youngstown you put people in the ground, out at Calvary under the snow, and every spring the frost heaves the stones a little crooked, and somebody goes out with a level. Here they keep them up in the air, in houses, on streets. On ground this low, that makes a kind of sense.
Lena knows the way without looking at the corners. Left, and left again, and halfway down a lane where the light comes in low between the rows, she stops.

It’s not one of the big ones. Two vaults, one over the other, a peaked roof with a small cross on it, GUIDRY cut over the door, and the marble tablets on the front with the names going down them, the oldest worn soft and the newest cut sharp. It’s white as a Sunday shirt, fresh, the whitewash still clean down into the corners and over the cracks.
“Wes did that,” she says. “Every All Saints since the storm. He did it this year too.” She touches the corner of the tomb with her knuckles. “Mémère asked him about the ring right here.”
Jack says nothing.

She takes the carnations out of his hands and lays them on the ledge under the names, newspaper and all, and works Laney’s gold strand off her wrist and lays it across them. She puts her hands back in her jacket. She tells her grandmother the score.

“Grandmère. *Trente et un, dix-sept.*” She says it to the newest name, the way her father reads the sports page at the table. “I know, I know, you don’t care, you never cared, I’m *telling* you anyway. *Écoute.*”
“Tell her about the onside kick.”

“I’m *getting* to the onside kick.” She doesn’t turn round. “Start of the second half, Grandmère. We kicked it short, on purpose, in the Super Bowl, and we got it back, and the house went up so loud Aints went under the table and wouldn’t come out till the fourth quarter.”
She stops, and wipes under her nose with the back of her wrist.
“She hated it,” she says, to Jack. “Football. All of it. She’d have been on the porch with Daddy and a rosary, saying it was a sin to want anything that much.”
“Was it?”
“She’d have been inside by the third quarter. Watching through the screen door.” She looks at the name. “Saying the rosary *for* them.”
A mockingbird is going on top of a tomb two lanes over, running through everything it knows. The low sun has got onto the GUIDRY tablet and the letters stand up out of it in shadow.

“She sewed,” Lena says. “For money, for people Uptown, hems and wedding dresses, in her front room with the pins in her mouth. She talked through them. She could tell you all about yourself with a mouthful of pins and you’d understand every word. She made the christening gown, the one we all wore. Luc first, in 1985. Then all of us. Lucille in January, and Lucille screamed through the entire Rite like she knew whose it was.” She smiles at the tablet. “She let me run the treadle on the old Singer when I was six. I sewed her apron to Mrs. Lacoste’s tablecloth. She wore it home like that, the apron and the tablecloth, to show Mama what I did.”
He laughs at that, and she looks at the tablet as though her grandmother had.

“She called me Magdalena. The whole name. Every time, even yelling.” She counts them off on the fingers of the hand at her side, not looking at them. “Grandmère. Mémère, when I’m in trouble. Father Hébert, because he poured the water.”

body.text: “Professor Hale, once, and I fixed that.”

body: “— and —”

She stops. Her hand hangs at her side with the names folded down into it and the next finger still up. She reaches down with the other one and turns a carnation on the ledge so its head faces the name.
The mockingbird does all the talking.
“I’ve never asked Mama one thing,” Lena says. “You know that.”
“I know.”
She nods, at the tomb. Out on Esplanade a bus pulls away from the stop with a long hiss of brakes.

She unbuttons the breast pocket of her jean jacket and takes out the medal. It rode home from Canal in there with the flap buttoned down over it, and the chain comes out after it in a little gold heap in her palm, the oval face of it turned up: Our Lady with her hands open and the rays coming off them, and the words round the edge. She tries the clasp. The ring at the end of the chain has sprung open in the crowd, and her fingers are red and stupid with cold, and she gets it in her nails and loses it, and gets it, and loses it again.
“Do it for me.”
She holds it out to him. She turns her back on him and on her grandmother’s name, and puts her other hand up and gathers her hair off her neck and holds it in a twist on top of her head.

He has the chain in his fingers. His hands are no better than hers, in this, but they were raised on Glenwood Avenue, on furnace filters and the pull chain of a garage door that came apart every winter, and he knows this ring. He gets it between his thumb and the side of his first finger and closes the gap with his thumbnail, a hair at a time, till the ends meet. He brings the chain round her from behind, the medal down in front of her, and holds the two ends at the back of her neck.

The back of her neck is cold. There’s the small knob of bone at the top of her spine, and a few short dark hairs that never make it into the twist, and the collar of the sweatshirt, and his own knuckles against her skin. She smells of the market and her shampoo. He could put his mouth there. He knows exactly how far it is. He has the clasp in his fingers, and her grandmother’s name over her shoulder, and he doesn’t.

choices.text: *Fasten it, and leave your hands there a second.*
choices.key: At her grandmother’s tomb in St. Louis No. 3 the clasp of Lena’s medal was broken. Do it for me, she said. You fastened it, and left your hands there a second.
response: He hooks the clasp through the ring, and it holds, and he doesn’t take his hands away. They stay where they ended up, on her shoulders at the base of her neck, over the collar.

She lets him. Her hand comes down out of her hair, and her hair comes down over his wrists, all of it, cold on the outside and warm underneath, and her hand comes over his on her shoulder and covers it, and holds it there.

When she turns round, under his hand, the medal is where it lives. She touches it, and looks at the tomb. “She said this at every gate she ever went through. Church. Here. The Schwegmann’s lot.” And she says what’s written round the edge: “*O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.*”
He says it after her.
The man in the cap is coming down the lane, rattling his keys for the last of the living. They go out the bayou side, and he locks the gate behind them.

choices.key: At her grandmother’s tomb in St. Louis No. 3 the clasp of Lena’s medal was broken. Do it for me, she said. You fastened it and stepped back.
response: He hooks the clasp through the ring, and tests it once with a tug, and it holds. He takes his hands back and steps off a pace and puts them in the pockets of the Carhartt.

Her hair comes down. She turns round. Her hand goes up to the medal at her collarbone and stays on it a moment, her thumb on the face of it, and she looks at him over it with her eyes very steady, and then at the tomb.

“She said this at every gate she ever went through,” she says. “Church. Here. The Schwegmann’s lot.” And she says it, the words round the edge: “*O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.*”
He says it after her, from where he’s standing.
At the end of the lane the man in the cap is shaking his keys at the tombs. They go out by the bayou side.

choices.key: At her grandmother’s tomb in St. Louis No. 3 the clasp of Lena’s medal was broken. You told her to hold still; she was shaking. It’s February in a cemetery, Jack.
response: Her shoulders are going under the sweatshirt, small and steady, and the chain jumps in his fingers with it.
“Hold still,” he says. “You’re shaking.”
“It’s cold.”
“It’s not that cold.”

“It’s February in a cemetery, Jack. It’s exactly that cold.” And she laughs, out loud, with her hair in her fist, loud enough that the mockingbird quits, and the laugh goes off down the lanes between the tombs, and he gets the clasp hooked while she’s still doing it.

She turns round with the medal where it lives, and puts her fingers on it, and is serious all at once. “She said this at every gate she ever went through. Church. Here. The Schwegmann’s lot.” And she says the words that run round the edge: “*O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.*”
He says it after her.
The man in the cap is coming down the lane with his keys, giving them a shake at every corner. They go out the bayou side, and he locks it after them.

s14.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:35 PM · BAYOU ST. JOHN, THE MAGNOLIA BRIDGE — DUEL (1)
body: The bayou is the last thing in the city to let go of the light. They have walked it the long way from the cemetery, because she wanted the light on the water, and every street off it has gone to shadow. Here it is, flat and dark and wider than he thought, with what’s left of the sky laid out on it, pale, and the trees on the far bank gone to one long dark shape.

The bridge is a low iron footbridge with a hump in the middle and a rail of flat bars, the rivets standing up in it like knuckles. They have it to themselves. Down on the bank a man in a hooded sweatshirt sits on an upturned bucket with a line in the water and a second bucket beside him and a transistor on its lid, still going on about yesterday to a man who isn’t listening. Out on the water a raft of small black birds with white bills paddles around in no order, one going under and coming up somewhere else, like a shift that has lost its foreman.

Lena gets up on the rail and sits on it, facing him, her back to the water, and hooks her boots under the bar below to hold herself on. Jack leans on the rail beside her, close enough to grab a sleeve. The iron is cold through the Carhartt, cold the way the chain-link at the Brier Hill gate is cold in February, a cold that has been out all day.
“The year after,” she says, “I came here before the seven o’clock and yelled at God off this bridge. Then I went to Mass and yelled at Him there.” She settles her boots. “He got it in stereo.”
“The year you went every morning.”
“Every morning. This was the warm-up.” She pats the bar under her. “Right here. Boots under that one so I wouldn’t go in. I had a lot to say and I wasn’t going to drown before I said it.”
“What’d He say back?”

“Mostly them.” She points her chin at the birds. “*Poules d’eau.* Water hens. Daddy’s brothers shoot them for gumbo. They taste like a liver that’s been to sea.” She watches one go under. “Today’s Scholastica.”
“*Sainte Scholastique.* Your grandmother turned the calendar.”
“Mémère turns it when there’s somebody in it worth turning for. Benedict had a sister. Not your Benedict. The first one. The one with the Rule.”
“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were about to say something about the Pope.” She is already off. “Scholastica. His twin, some people say, but Gregory doesn’t say it, so don’t quote me. She has her nuns, and he has his monks up the mountain, and once a year he comes down to a little house near the monastery and they spend the day together. Praising God. Talking holy. All day, the one day they get.”
“Like Thanksgiving.”

“Like Thanksgiving if anybody at Thanksgiving ever got to finish a sentence. So it gets dark. They eat. They’re still going. And she says, Brother, don’t leave me tonight. Stay, and we’ll talk about heaven till morning. And he says —” her voice drops down into her chest, into a man who has been up since Matins and would like his bed — “*What are you saying, sister? I can’t stay. I have a Rule.*”

She doesn’t argue with him, Lena says. She folds her hands on her knee, there on the rail, and puts her forehead down on them, and stays like that while a bird goes under and comes up and goes under again.
“What’d she pray?”

“Gregory doesn’t say. Gregory was a gentleman.” She comes up. “The sky’s clear. Not a cloud in it. He’s very particular about that. Clear sky, and she lifts her head off her hands, and it *opens*. Thunder. Lightning. Rain so hard he can’t put a foot out the door, him or the brothers he brought. And Benedict says, God forgive you, sister. What have you done? And she says —” and here the voice goes small and sweet, a girl with all night — “*I asked you, and you wouldn’t listen. So I asked my God, and He did. Go now, if you can. Go on back to your monastery.*”
Jack laughs.

“So he stays,” Lena says. “They talk all night about heaven.” She is looking up the bayou now, toward the lake, and she has quit doing the voices. “Three days later she’s dead. He’s in his cell and he looks up and sees her go, like a dove, straight into heaven. He put her in the tomb he’d had made for himself.” She turns back to him. “It’s the only miracle in Gregory where God takes a side against a saint. And He takes hers.”

choices.text: “He had a Rule. He’d promised. You argued once that a promise is made to a person, not to a reason.”
response: Her mouth comes open. “You *kept* that? I wrote on your paper you didn’t believe one sentence of it. And neither did I.”
“You wrote it in pen.”

“It was *your* pen.” Out on the water a bird runs along the top of the bayou, slapping, trying to get up, and gives it up and settles where it started. When she comes back to him she’s serious. “I’ve come round. A promise is made to a person. And his sister is a person. The Rule isn’t.”
She counts it off on two fingers, person, reason. The pale is going off the water.

choices.text: “She went over his head to his boss.”
response: She shrieks, loud enough that the fisherman on the bank looks up from his line.
“She went over his head to *her* boss,” Lena says, lower, with her boots kicking. “Same boss. That’s the *point*.”

choices.text: “She got one day a year. I’d have prayed for the storm too.”
response: She looks at him. On the bank behind her a big old house with two stories of galleries puts on a light upstairs, and then one down, and the galleries come up out of the dark a window at a time, white posts and black screens.
“You would have,” she says. “You’d have prayed for hail.”
“Hail’s a sure thing.”
“Hail’s a *sin*, in February, on a poor man’s monastery.” She hooks her boots back under the bar, tighter.

choices.text: “It’s not the Rule against the sister. It’s whose prayer gets answered.”
response: “Hers. That’s what I *said*.”
“No. You said God took a side. I’m saying He answered a prayer. He didn’t answer Benedict’s because Benedict didn’t make one.”
She opens her mouth, and shuts it, and points at him. “Hold that.”

s14a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:55 PM · THE MAGNOLIA BRIDGE — DUEL (2)
body: The light goes out of the bayou from the bottom up. The water goes first, then the far bank, then the trees on it, until there is nothing out there but the sky, and the house on the bank with every one of its galleries lit now, and the radio on the bucket lid down to a murmur somebody has turned low. The birds have gone in somewhere. Lena’s knee is against his arm where he leans on the rail, and has been since the storm opened, and he hasn’t moved the arm.

A man comes over the hump of the bridge at a jog, in a gold Brees jersey over a sweatshirt, with a little lamp strapped to his forehead, and they make room for him: she swings her knees toward the water and Jack steps in against the rail. “Who dat,” the man says, going by, not even winded. “Who dat,” says Lena. His lamp goes bobbing off down the far side toward Moss Street, and Jack is standing closer than he was, with her knee against his hip now instead of his arm.

“I like Benedict,” she says. “Don’t make that face. I *like* him. He wrote a chapter on how much wine a monk gets, and he apologizes in it. Wine is no drink for monks, he says, but since you can’t convince monks of that nowadays, a little. That’s a man who has met monks.”
“He’d have done fine at Sully’s.”

“He’d have *run* Sully’s. That’s my point. He isn’t a hard man. He’s a man who knows exactly how soft people are and writes it down so they can stand to live in one house.” She holds up a finger in the dark, a point of order. “The Rule says the abbot should try to be loved rather than feared. He wrote that. Chapter sixty-four. And he couldn’t love his sister one night past the bell.”
Jack has read the Rule, or the parts of it anybody reads, and he can’t find chapter sixty-four anywhere in him, and she sits there on the rail with her finger up and watches him look for it.

choices.text: “The Rule is love too. There were men back at the monastery waiting on him to keep it.”
response: Her boots come down off the rail onto the bridge.
“Then he should’ve gone home in the rain,” she says, evenly. “He didn’t. He *stayed*.”

choices.text: “Gregory was a Benedictine. He’s grading his own abbot.”
response: She sits straight up on the rail, lit, the way she gets when somebody is wrong in exactly the place she happens to be standing. “Gregory was a monk in his own house in Rome, St. Andrew’s, and there’s no proving whose Rule they kept. You’re grading a man on a rumor.”
“I’m grading him on a storm.”
“You’re grading him on a storm you weren’t *at*.” She hooks her boots back under the bar.

choices.text: “She knew it was the last time. He didn’t.”
response: Lena takes her hands out of her sleeves and holds them together in her lap.
“Three days,” she says, low. “*That’s* the argument.”
She looks at him over them, and he looks back.

choices.text: “He kept the Rule. God made it impossible to break. Everybody got what they asked for.”
response: She thinks about it with her chin down in the collar of the jean jacket.
“That’s Jesuitical.”
“I’m from Youngstown. We’re all Jesuits.”
“You went to *Mooney*.”
“Mooney’s very open-minded.”
She pulls the jacket collar up over her mouth and says something into it in French that he is fairly sure is not a compliment, and fairly sure is not an insult either.

s14b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:15 PM · THE MAGNOLIA BRIDGE — DUEL (3), FINAL
body: By the time either of them has anything left, it’s nearly night. The galleries on the bank have gone yellow and the bayou under them is ink, and the fisherman has his rod across his knees and his second bucket shut.

body.text: When she calls it, it’s low, to the water, and not to him. “She could do more, because she loved more.”
She calls it with her chin up out of her collar. “Benedict wins on the Rule.”
“And she gets the night,” Jack says.
“She gets the *night*.”
“You argued that like a man throwing hail,” she says. “I’m calling it a draw, and only because you made me laugh. Twice.”
“I’ll take twice.”
“You’d have stood out in the rain to win the point,” she says.
“I’d have stayed in to win it.”
“Then you’d have lost it twice.” She doesn’t gloat, much. “That one’s mine.”
“You’d have stood out in the rain to win the point,” she says.
“I’d have stayed in to win it.”
“Then it’s a draw,” she says, “and the rain’s not here to settle it.”
She’s already standing, her back against the rail. She tips her head back on it and looks up, and so does he.
body.else: She unhooks her boots and gets down off the rail and turns round to it beside him, and looks up, and so does he.

body: Over the bayou the sky is clear. It came down black from the top while they argued, faster than it does at home, and the city keeps a dull orange going round the bottom edge of it, but straight up it’s hard and clean, the first stars out in it, and low in the east there’s one too red to be a star that doesn’t blink. No moon. Not a rag of cloud anywhere, not over the lake, not over the rooftops, not over the cemetery behind them with its gate locked. The water doesn’t move. Down on the bank the fisherman is winding in.
They look at it. Nothing comes.
“Well,” Lena says. “I didn’t ask.”
The rail is cold under his forearms. He leaves them on it.

choices.key: On the Magnolia Bridge after the argument about Scholastica, the sky stayed clear. Well, Lena said. I didn’t ask. You told her she didn’t have to.
response: She comes along the rail until her shoulder is against his, through the jean jacket and the Carhartt both, the warmest thing on the bridge, and stands there until the man with the bucket has gone up the bank with both buckets and the radio and his rod over his shoulder.
When they go it’s down the hump of the bridge toward Moss Street, the dark come down over everything, and at the bottom she takes his arm, his elbow in both hands, and keeps it.

choices.text: “Gregory would’ve thrown in hail for you.”
choices.key: On the Magnolia Bridge the sky stayed clear. Well, Lena said. I didn’t ask. You told her Gregory would have thrown in hail for her. Gregory was a romantic, she said.
response: “Gregory was a romantic.” She pushes off the rail. “You don’t write four books of miracles if you’re not. You write a pamphlet.”
“You’d have liked him.”
“I’d have *edited* him.”

She takes his sleeve, a fistful of Carhartt cuff, the way you’d take a boy who’s about to wander off at a second line, and walks him off the bridge toward Moss Street like that, down the hump in the dark, and doesn’t let go of it at the bottom.

choices.text: Look at the sky with her, and say nothing.
choices.key: On the Magnolia Bridge the sky stayed clear. Well, Lena said. I didn’t ask. You looked at the sky with her and said nothing.
response: He looks at it with her. The red one in the east stays red. Behind them the fisherman goes up the bank with his buckets and his radio, and a car goes by on Moss Street with its windows up and its bass going, and then that’s gone too, and it’s the two of them and the iron and the sky, until her teeth are going.

“Supper,” she says, as if that were the end of an argument, and they walk off the bridge toward Moss Street close enough that her shoulder knocks his on the way down the hump, and keeps knocking it, to the corner and round it.

s15.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:30 PM → 9:50 PM · MID-CITY — THE LONG WAY ROUND
body: The supper place is a corner bar on Bienville with a kitchen in the back and a Barq’s sign in the window that has lost the bottom of its *s*. Inside it smells of fry oil and Pine-Sol: the bar down one wall with a television over the end of it, six tables down the other in red oilcloth, and by the bathroom door a jukebox with its colors going round. Two men in Entergy jackets are at the bar with their elbows either side of their beers. At the far end of it a woman in a Saints sweatshirt is doing the *Picayune* crossword in pen.

Lena doesn’t give him a menu. She gives the man behind the bar the order from across the room, a whole muffuletta, warm, and two Barq’s in the bottle, and when it comes out on butcher paper she cuts it in four with the bread knife that comes with it and takes the biggest quarter, and puts the second-biggest in front of him. Manners. It’s the size of a hubcap, sesame on top and the oil off the olive salad soaked clean through the bottom. Nonna would have opinions about olives on a sandwich, all of them in Italian, and would eat two quarters.
“Well?” Lena says.
“Ask me after the second quarter.”
“That *is* your second quarter.”
He looks down at his paper. It is. “It’s good,” he says, with his mouth full, and she nods as though she cooked it.

Over the bar the television has the news on with the sound off. The parade again, from a helicopter, Canal Street black with people from one side to the other under the lights; a man at a desk with a stack of papers he doesn’t look at. Then, across the bottom of the screen in white letters beside the five rings: VANCOUVER 2010, and a count of days to go: two. Lena looks up at it with her quarter halfway to her mouth. Jack looks up at it too. It goes to the weather, a map of the Gulf with nothing on it, clear and cold up to the lake, and she takes her bite.

While she’s buttoning the jean jacket at the door, somebody at the bar feeds the jukebox, and the Neville Brothers come on, slow, Aaron’s voice going up past the television, higher than a man’s voice has any business going, and the two men in the Entergy jackets quit talking to let it.
Outside she turns left. Dupre Street is to the right: five days in this city and he knows that much. He goes left with her.

It’s full dark and cold, and there are more stars out over the rooflines than Glenwood Avenue gets all February. The side streets back here are narrow and quiet, the houses close up to the sidewalk on their piers, shotguns and doubles and a camelback here and there, a porch light on every third one. He starts to see the lines, and once he’s seen one he can’t stop. On most of the houses it’s gone under new paint, and you’d only know it was there because the paint below the porch rail is a shade brighter than the paint above, like a wall where a picture used to hang. On some it’s been left. A yellow double with green shutters wears it on purpose, a brown stripe straight across the front at the height of a man’s chest, and somebody has lettered under it, small and neat in white, *8·29·05*, and hung the flower boxes right below that, full of pansies. Two doors down there’s a line with a fainter line a foot under it, where the water stood a week, and went down a foot, and stood again.
Somewhere after the yellow double her hand has come through his arm, and her shoulder is against his, and they walk like that.

Halfway down the next block there is a house whose people never came back. The windows are plywood gone gray. The porch roof sags in the middle like a hammock, and grass has come up through the treads of the steps. By the front door, on the siding, is a big X in orange spray paint gone pale with weather, with something written into each of its four corners: a date at the top, letters on one side, letters on the other, which he can’t read and she doesn’t read for him. In the bottom corner there is a 0.
Lena stops on the sidewalk in front of it.
“Zero’s the good number,” she says.
She walks on, and he walks with her.
At the next corner he looks back over his shoulder, toward the bayou. “It came from there?”

“Everybody thinks the bayou.” She takes her hand back out of his arm and turns him by the sleeve to face the other way, up the dark street toward the lake, where there’s nothing to see but a streetlight and a cat crossing under it. “The canals. Seventeenth Street. London Avenue. The walls gave out, and this city’s tipped toward the lake like Mémère’s kitchen floor: drop a pea by the stove and it ends up at the back door. So it came in at the low end and filled from there, like a sink, till it got all the way up to us.” She lets go of his sleeve. “Wes could tell you to the inch. He’s going to build the walls right.”
“Good,” Jack says.

She wants Youngstown, block by block, and he tells it. The lines there aren’t water. You can tell the year a street gave up by its paint. Out along the river where the Sheet & Tube was there’s a stretch of chain-link with a gate in it and nothing behind the gate but sumac, and every time Pop drives Nonna past it she makes him slow the truck down, and crosses herself.
“For the mill,” Lena says.

“For my grandfather. To her it’s the same thing.” Sunday gravy at two. Not two-oh-five. At two-oh-five Nonna has said grace without you, and you say it again standing up, by yourself, with the table watching and Gina timing you on the microwave clock.
“That’s Mémère with the rosary. You come in on the third decade, you start over from the Creed, with her counting.”

body.text: He tells her about Rosie’s dinosaur, the green one from the gift shop at Cabazon, riding home to Glenwood Avenue in his duffel, and the name on the box they took away, and that Jude knows, and isn’t telling, and Rosie can’t ever. Lena hears him out with her hands in her jacket.
“How old is she?”
“Eight.”
“Then she doesn’t hear it from me.” She spits in her palm, neatly, the way Mémère does business with the man who sells her satsumas, and holds it out, and he shakes on it.
He tells her Jude asked him whether Ohio has dinosaurs.
“What’d you tell him?”
“Trilobites.”
She shakes her head at the sidewalk. “That boy’s going to think about that till Easter.”

body: “How’s Danny?”
“He said watch the game. All of it.”
“Did you?”
“All of it.”
She nods. A little farther on she asks what he’s giving Hale.
“You first.”
“The bag.”
“Four thousand words on a Schwegmann’s bag.”
“On penance. In a bag. He said nothing about football. He never said a word about bags.” She looks up at him. “You?”
“The second line.”

body.text: “You haven’t been in one.”
body.else: “You’ve been in one.”

body.text: “Not yet.”
body.else: “One.”

body.text: “Then you owe me another one.”
body.else: “Then you owe me a second line.”

body: A block on, under a streetlight, she says, “Laney’s been crossing herself. She’s *Baptist*.”
“Theo gave Kevin his phone.”
Lena stops dead under the light. “Lord. What did they *do*?”
“I was going to ask you.”

She looks at him, and he looks at her, and they have nothing, either of them, and she takes his arm again and they go on. At the corner she turns left again. A block after that they pass a corner store with burglar bars and a hand-lettered sign in the window for hot boudin, and he would swear on Nonna’s gravy that they passed it an hour ago, from the other side.

choices.text: “This isn’t the way to the house.”
response: “This isn’t the way to the house,” he says.
“It’s *a* way,” Lena says.

She doesn’t change it. She takes them two more blocks wrong and one back, under a wire with a pair of sneakers hung over it by the laces, and at last round onto Dupre Street, where halfway down the block every window in her mother’s house is lit.
“Juan Diego,” he says.
She looks at him sideways, under the burglar bars. “Juan Diego was in a hurry.”
“And you?”
“I’m not.”

She walks on with her hand through his arm. It’s three more blocks, all of them the wrong way, before they come round the last corner onto Dupre Street and see the house down the block with its porch light on and the Odyssey at the curb.
They walk.

The sidewalks back here are broken into slabs by the roots, heaved up and tipped every which way, and she knows where every one of them is and steps over it with her eyes on the street, and by the second block he has learned them too. When they turn onto Dupre Street at last the house is lit from end to end, down the block, the Odyssey dark at the curb in front of it.

s16.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:05 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE SIDE YARD — THE LINE
body: They don’t go up the steps. Lena goes past the foot of them and in at the gate in the chain-link along the side of the lot, by the trash cans, and holds it for him, and as he comes round the corner of the house the porch is above them, lit.

Theo is in Tony’s kitchen chair, the one that lives out there, in the good coat with the collar up. Tony is beside him on the swing in a Saints windbreaker with a cup of chicory going cold on his knee. The transistor sits on the rail on its coat-hanger antenna, playing WWL low, a man calling in from Chalmette, and Tony has the radio turned square to his face. The two of them are just sitting. Behind them, in the front window, the curtain is held back by one finger, and the face beside the finger is Laney’s, with Mémère’s lamp on behind her.

All three of them look at Jack and Lena coming up the side yard. Then all three look away at once: Theo at the street, with two quick knocks of his knuckles on the arm of the kitchen chair; Tony at the radio; and the curtain falling shut.

body.text: The kitchen window throws a yellow square across the grass to the back of the lot. Lena walks into it and out the far side of it to the shed, and puts her back to the boards, against the line he has had his hand on.
body.else: The kitchen window throws a yellow square across the grass to the back of the lot. Lena walks into it and out the far side of it to the shed, and puts her back to the boards, against the line she showed him with her phone.

body: She leans there in the Broussard’s Seafood sweatshirt and the jean jacket, at the edge of the light, and the line crosses her at the collarbone. The medal he fastened at four o’clock lies on it, outside the collar of the sweatshirt, on its mended chain, and catches the window.

He stands in front of her. Up close her face is still pink from the wind off the bayou, and there’s a fleck of gold at her hairline, left from Tuesday’s paint, that two washings haven’t found. She has been talking all evening, and now she isn’t. The cold is coming up out of the grass into his boots. On the porch the man from Chalmette is laughing at something on the telephone, and the house behind him is going quiet for the night, room by room.
Her hand comes up out of her jacket pocket and lies flat across his chest, over the Carhartt, at the height the line would be on him.
“Here,” she says.

She leaves it there. Her palm is cold through the canvas, and then it isn’t. He wants her, standing in a dark yard with her back to the shed and her grandmother’s medal on the waterline, and his hands stay in his pockets. They’ve been there the length of Mid-City. She looks up at him in the yellow light, and keeps her hand where it is.

response: “I’m here,” he says.

Her hand doesn’t move for a long time. On the porch the radio goes to a commercial for a mattress store and comes back. Her fingers close on the canvas, a fistful of the Carhartt, and hold it, and let it go, and then her hand comes off his chest and back into her pocket, and the cold comes in where it was.

response: He takes his right hand out of his pocket and puts it over hers, and keeps it there. Her hand is under his and his heart is under hers, and the kitchen light is on them both, and on the line behind her, and on the medal.
When she takes her hand back she slides it out from under his slowly, a knuckle at a time, and his hand is left on his own coat where hers was.
